We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that combines the benefits of neural networks and descriptor fields to enable efficient and robust manipulation tasks. NDFs incorporate both local and global features that capture an object's intricate details and its overall shape, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding. We incorporate a novel orientation-agnostic matching technique that utilizes a contrastive loss function to compare an object to a reference shape, effectively capturing its intrinsic properties. In contrast to object-based manipulation approaches that rely heavily on precise object recognition, NDFs focus on an object's intrinsic descriptors that are insensitive to its orientation, allowing for more flexible task execution. We demonstrate the utility of NDFs in a range of manipulation tasks involving oriented objects by simply redefining the success criterion as an orientation-agnostic descriptor matching problem. Our results show that NDFs-based solutions outperform industry standards in various evaluation metrics. The code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/PranavTiwari-NLP/NeuralDescriptorFields.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct tasks: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We integrated projection grouping and correspondence learning models using a unified loss function with a bridge module that connects them, and experimented with multiple combinations of models. Our proposed approach, named DeepHMap++, was applied to the BOP Toolkit. Our findings indicate that combining projection grouping and correspondence learning models leads to improved results, with an overall accuracy of 85.3% for the Easy dataset and 53.4% for the Hard dataset. Furthermore, we discovered that selecting intermediate cues in two-stage pipelines through the use of quality scores rather than randomness generates more accurate results. Our code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/lingyu2016/DeepHMap++.

Generalized Graphical Lasso, a method for inferring nodal connections in multi-layered networks, has been extensively utilized in various applications. However, the availability of a comprehensive and user-friendly Python library to seamlessly integrate various GGLasso implementations, available in optimized C++ tools, has been a hindrance for researchers. To address this gap, we present GGLasso, a Python-based library that incorporates multiple highly efficient C++ algorithms for computing Generalized Graphical Lasso on graph data, including an innovative semi-Newton method, an APG algorithm, and an interface to the highly optimized BPDENET C++ implementation. Furthermore, GGLasso offers a range of useful features, including the ability to balance sparsity and node degree, multi-core CPU utilization for faster computation, and support for large-scale datasets via the BPDENET C++ implementation available in Python through the bdpy module. We demonstrate the performance and versatility of GGLasso through various network analysis tasks, including multi-layered network clustering, biomolecular network learning, and sparse regression. The source code for GGLasso is available at https://github.com/alexisgobard/GGLasso.

This study investigates how spheres interact with running water by being pressed into contact with a flowing water surface. This research was motivated by its relevance to various scenarios involving water and solid interfaces, such as in pipes, on slopes, and with partially submerged objects. Previous studies primarily examined high-speed regimes where the water pressure beneath the sphere is similar to the atmospheric pressure, or slow-speed regimes where the sphere takes an extended time to enter the water completely. This study focuses on intermediate speed regimes, where the sphere's speed is sufficient to enter the water quickly, but not fast enough to prevent water from entering the gap between the sphere and the water surface. The factors influencing this interaction are the sphere's size, surface roughness, and density, as well as the water flow rate and surface tension of the water. A comprehensive understanding of this interaction is presented through experimental observations, with the development of a mathematical model to predict the behavior of spheres in water flowing interfaces. This model considers the forces driving the sphere into the water, the friction it encounters, and the pressure exerted by the water on its underside. By analyzing how the sphere's density, size, and surface roughness affect its interaction with the water, this study provides equations that can be used to predict when the sphere will start to enter the water, when it will be completely submerged, and how the water will flow over the sphere once it is submerged. This research also examines how changing the water flow rate, surface tension, and the presence of a thin film of air on the water surface influence the sphere's interaction with the water. Our investigation uses first-principles calculations to examine the orbital characteristics of cupricite, a rare mineral with the formula CuFe2S3, and the effects of electron-correlation and strain on its crystals. Due to the unique arrangement of its atoms in the crystal structure, cupricite exhibits a small band gap in its energy spectrum. Our findings show that this gap results from the interaction of a p-type orbital from the copper atom and the p-type orbitals from the oxygen atoms, rather than the t2g or eg orbitals typical of transition metal oxides. This distinctive feature makes cupricite an unusual example of a transition metal sulfide with a direct gap. Our results also demonstrate that the electrons' behavior can vary depending on the direction normal to the (001) plane in which the energy levels are measured, indicating that the electrons' behavior differs depending on the orbital in three-dimensional space. This unique orbital behavior could be a general principle of physics, applicable to all atoms arranged in similar structures anywhere in the universe. Our calculations suggest that the electrons' behavior can be influenced by applying pressure or releasing it, which alters the bond lengths between the atoms and changes the energy levels in the orbitals. However, the effects of these changes on the material's magnetic properties and energy levels are complex and vary depending on the perspective from which they are viewed. Nonetheless, our findings show that the application of pressure or releasing it in the x, y, or z directions normal to the (001) plane alters the energy levels in the t2g or eg orbitals differently. For instance, when pressure is applied in the z direction normal to the (001) plane, it increases the bond lengths between the atoms, causing the energy levels in the t2g or eg orbitals to move further apart than in the x or y directions. On the other hand, releasing the pressure in the z direction normal to the (001) plane decreases the bond lengths between the atoms, causing the energy levels in the t2g or eg orbitals to move closer together than in the x or y directions. Our investigation focuses on the 2D non-symmorphic wallpaper structure composed of hexagons and rectangles to explore its electronic properties. By utilizing a first-principles calculation method, we discovered a distinctive feature - a adjustable Dirac point located at the K point in the reciprocal space. This point can be steered through the electronic phase transition of this material, resulting from the adjustment of an external pressure or electric field. As a notable aspect, we discovered that the adjustable Dirac point behaves uniquely in the lattice, exhibiting rotation in the real space in response to the change in orientation of the lattice structure. This interconnection between the geometry, electron composition, and the spatial arrangement of atoms allows us to tailor the adjustable Dirac point by modifying the wallpaper structure. In particular, we suggest changing the hexagon to a square, which would move the location of the Dirac point from the K point to the $\Gamma$ point in the reciprocal space. In this new configuration, the migration of the Dirac point is linked to the migration of a charge disproportionation, which can be managed by adjusting an external pressure or electric field. Notably, both of these wallpaper structures possess ferromagnetic properties, ensuring that the location of the Dirac point remains stable in the superconducting phase. In the square structure, we observed the appearance of four adjustable Dirac points in the reciprocal space, primarily located at the M points. These results are expected to contribute to the development of controllable topological materials. We also suggest possible materials that incorporate this unique property, including phosphorus terminated MoTe2, which offers an alternative method of creating adjustable Dirac points through the adjustment of an external electric field or pressure on the Te layer. Our study indicates that both of these materials possess the square structure and MoTe2 contains both the adjustable Dirac points and the charge disproportionation, allowing for the management of the Dirac points by adjusting the composition of the Te layer. Our data were verified through an experimental method, using a scanning tunneling microscopy to visualize the arrangement of atoms, a photoemission spectroscopy to analyze the composition of the electrons, and a transport measurement to examine the magnetic and superconducting properties. Our findings have been applied to predict the behavior of other transition metal dichalcogenides that contain the 2D non-symmorphic wallpaper structure, allowing for the creation of materials that incorporate the unique property of the adjustable Dirac points. Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states have interesting properties, being resistant to decoherence while facilitating the interaction between a quantum system and a light field. These states could be advantageous for various quantum information applications. However, generating them proves challenging using traditional methods due to their high requirement for contrast ratios. A quantum-optical catalysis process using Squeezed Light as a catalyst to generate these states might offer a solution, and this study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method, explaining how to set the parameters of the catalyst and the initial state of a quantum system to produce the desired states efficiently. Additionally, we examine the effectiveness of this process and provide guidelines for scaling it to larger quantum systems. This approach has the potential to make single-photon facilitated coherent states more accessible in experiments. This study also showcases a feasible implementation using superconducting resonators, offering a promising future integration with other systems. Moreover, we explore the connection between this process and ancilla-driven coherent measurement, discussing its potential in enabling scalable quantum computation. We introduce a technique for creating polynomial models using linear regression as a foundation.  This approach, which we refer to as PROPS (Polynomial Construction using Regression and Integer Optimization for Synthesis), leverages linear regression to determine polynomial coefficients. Code-mixed language refers to text that combines two or more languages, a common practice especially among multilingual populations who navigate different linguistic domains, such as online social platforms, signs and instructions within border regions, and cultural events. Despite the prevalence of code-mixed language, research in NLP has historically focused on monolingual approaches, neglecting the intricate challenges it presents. This issue explores recent advancements in NLP involving code-mixed data, with an emphasis on techniques for categorizing social media posts, with additional discussion on other applications including sentiment analysis, sentence translation, and generation. We also examine challenges posed by code-mixed data, potential datasets, and strategies for evaluating models. Current developments primarily pertain to Hindi-English code-mixed data, though future research may explore other language combinations. We highlight key challenges, research opportunities, and future directions for NLP involving code-mixed data, with a specific focus on techniques for categorizing social media posts, but note similar challenges apply to other applications and combinations of languages. We conclude with discussions on crucial issues including usability, ethics, and operational feasibility of NLP systems using code-mixed data. Reddit's vast community allows for diverse discussions to take place within subgroups, based on users' personal connections, occupations, or geographic locations. Prior studies classify users into the Big Four Groups: political, occupational, interest-based, and geographic. Our research examines the significance of categorizing users by geographic location within Reddit, often overlooked in misinformation studies. We propose the term "Big Geographic Sort" to describe this classification. The study determines the Big Geographic Sort's implications for misinformation spread by identifying correlations between user group classifications, analyzing the impact of misinformation post engagement on users, modeling the rate at which users engage with misinformation, and exploring user characteristics and demographics. Our findings reveal that users sorted by geography are more likely to engage with misinformation than those sorted by interest or occupation, yet less likely than those sorted by politics. Furthermore, we discover that users sorted by geography exhibit different levels of misinformation engagement based on their location, with urban users more susceptible to misinformation than rural users. The study highlights the importance of considering the Big Geographic Sort in understanding and analyzing misinformation dissemination within Reddit. We also propose possible explanations for the significance of the Big Geographic Sort, including the overlap between interest-based and occupational groups, the varied levels of urban isolation among Reddit users, and the influence of moderators on subgroups based on geographic location. The study's conclusions can be expanded to broader online platforms beyond Reddit. We anticipate that the term Big Geographic Sort will facilitate future research on the subject, encompassing the study of misinformation, online communities, and social connections. The study's findings can be applied to develop strategies for reducing misinformation dissemination within Reddit, as well as similar online platforms, by targeting user groups sorted by geographic location. The research paper also explores the issue of misinformation from a social connectivity perspective, highlighting the value of analyzing fake news spreads within Reddit, based on user connections, moderation practices, and geographic location. The study's results can be utilized by developers of online platforms, such as Reddit, to implement measures that combat misinformation dissemination within user groups sorted by geographic location. Humans naturally generate rich auditory feedback while interacting with their environment, which significantly enhances the understanding of their intentions and actions.  Despite the prevalence of auditory feedback during human activity, developing robotic systems that can efficiently comprehend and interpret this feedback remains a challenge.  This issue is particularly pronounced in scenarios where robots are responsible for learning from human instructors through observation and auditory feedback.  This paper presents an investigation of the auditory patterns produced by human instructors as they carry out manipulation tasks in front of robots.  Specifically, this study assesses the overall structure and content of audio feedback, considering elements such as speech, non-speech sounds, and ambient noise.  Sixteen volunteers participated in a demonstration exercise in front of a robot, incorporating six different demonstration methods: three conventional approaches (using objects with different sizes and shapes, and a screwdriver) and three more challenging scenarios (with moving robots, on smooth surfaces, and in a noisy environment).  The results show that the audio feedback generated during the demonstrations varies considerably, with a notable observation being that the majority of sound emissions originate from the hands and fingers of the instructors.  The research also examines the relationship between audio feedback and the physical activity performed by the instructor, presenting an analytical framework for assessing this connection.  The findings have implications for designing robotic systems that can learn from human instructors through observation and auditory feedback, and the proposed research can be integrated into existing approaches to enhance the understanding of audio feedback.  The study's data has been made available to the scientific community via a public repository, along with an appendix containing additional information about the results.  The paper also discusses potential applications and challenges in the health and robotics industries, citing the case of a robotic system that can learn from audio feedback to assist with physical therapy.  The research has been conducted within the framework of the Robot Activity Understanding Through Auditory Feedback (RAUF) project.  The data collected during this study can be utilized to develop a system that extracts relevant audio feedback from demonstrations, along with a concept called the Auditory Activity Matrix (AAM).  The AAM provides a comprehensive analysis of the audio feedback generated during demonstrations, examining the relationship between the instructor's actions and the audio feedback produced.  The paper also presents an approach to develop such a system, along with the AAM framework, and outlines potential future work, along with the RAUF project's background and related research.  The study has further been validated through an experiment involving the automated extraction of audio feedback from demonstrations, along with the AAM framework, by two separate groups

Creating conversational agents like chatbots requires a structured approach. This paper focuses on a automated testing framework for conversational systems, which it terms as "Machine Testing Systems" or "MTS". We outline the fundamental components of MTS, citing examples from a hypothetical user. Next, we outline the method for developing an automated testing framework for conversational systems, ending with a discussion on the system's testing methodology, the testing methodology consisting of initial setup, ongoing testing, and termination criteria. We also examine various MTS components, breaking them down into essential parts that include input data, system components, and output data. Finally, we examine the testing methodology of MTS at length, detailing eight distinct methods that include evaluation of multiple outcomes, systematic evaluation, as well as thorough testing among others. We conclude by examining research opportunities in the field of MTS. This paper was originally published in the proceedings of the IEEE WACN 2005 conference.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target scenarios are common paradigms used in cross-domain recommendation. In the single-target setting, recommendations are made for one user with multiple preferences across different domains, whereas in the dual-target setting, recommendations are made for both a user and an item across different domains. However, both of these scenarios have limitations and cannot be applied to real-world scenarios by themselves. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel MSDCR algorithm that engages in multiple-sparse-domain cooperative recommendation. In this framework, there is an overarching framework with multiple domains, and we consider a sub-set of these domains to be relevant for making recommendations about a particular user. Our objective is to identify this sub-set of relevant domains. We achieve this by implementing a two-phase approach. First, we identify the preferred domains by determining the degree of density existence $\delta$ in each domain. We calculate $\delta$ as the ratio of active item IDs to the total number of IDs in a particular domain. Next, we establish a threshold $\delta_t$ that serves as a baseline for distinguishing between sparse and dense domains. We recommend selecting the top N domains with densities greater than $\delta_t$ as the preferred domains. By dividing a wide bandwidth into narrowband signals, these models also offer reduced power levels, increased sensitivity, and improved carrier differentiation. We show that both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM solutions can be applied in a flexible and adaptive manner, allowing them to be used in various scenarios, including 5G NR. Moreover, these schemes can be implemented using readily available baseband and RF equipment, and are compatible with existing standards and infrastructure. We also explore and present optimized design criteria for these models, as well as simulated results for various SISO and MISO configurations. In addition, we introduce a novel concept called "Overlapping Waveforming," which enables multiple WBWFC structures to overlap and combine their benefits in a single network. In contrast to non-overlapping designs, this approach offers greater flexibility, faster adaptation rates, and the ability to operate in a "blind manner" with other networks. We believe that both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM schemes have significant value and could be used in their own right in various applications, not just as equivalents of the WBWFC structure. In multiagent competitions, players' motivations can be driven by a mix of cooperative and self-serving intentions. We are interested in identifying the rationalizable equilibria resulting from repeated interactions among players following cooperative and self-serving behaviors. We establish conditions under which the set of rationalizable strategies in repeated games can be obtained from a single stage game through the use of universal mechanisms applicable to various degrees of self-serving behavior. We also examine how players' motivations influence the stability of cooperative behaviors in different scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the incorporation of mechanisms such as commitment or reinforcement learning can lead to the convergence of rationalizable equilibria in repeated games. In addition, we discuss a notable exception where a specific game fails to converge to a rationalizable equilibrium, thereby highlighting the importance of suitable mechanisms in ensuring convergence. In examining these issues, we utilize a particular multiagent competition game as a key example to analyze the relationship between cooperative and self-serving intentions. This includes the examination of how cooperative intentions influence the stability of the strategy space as well as the way in which the population's level of self-serving behavior affects the convergence to a rationalizable equilibrium. We also provide a characterization of the set of rationalizable strategies that is achievable in a single stage game, thereby providing a precise understanding of the relationship between cooperative intentions, the availability of mechanisms, and the level of self-serving behavior on the resulting rationalizable equilibria. This characterization enables us to identify two distinct regimes of cooperative intentions, one of which is associated with a collective cooperation while the other is characterized by collective defection. We further examine a specific example of a dynamic game where cooperation is initially established through cooperation, only to deteriorate into complete defection due to the level of self-serving behavior exhibited by the players. This example enables us to illustrate the complex relationship between cooperative intentions, the availability of mechanisms, and the level of self-serving behavior on the resulting rationalizable equilibria in multiagent competitions. This is further reinforced by the fact that a gradual increase in the level of self-serving behavior exhibited by the players, from a level where cooperation is established to a level where cooperation fails to be sustained, occurs without any abrupt transition, thereby indicating that the transition between the two regimes of cooperative intentions on the resulting rationalizable equilibria in multiagent competitions is continuous rather than discrete. This finding is particularly significant because it enables us to extend the results we have obtained to date by examining the relationship between cooperative intentions, the availability of mechanisms, and the level of self-serving behavior on the resulting rationalizable equilib

An epidemic spread can lead a network to undergo significant changes, potentially causing it to shed infected nodes that are connected to healthy ones in an attempt to contain the outbreak. We have examined how networks respond to an epidemic by removing infected nodes with weak connections to preserve connectivity to healthy nodes. We developed mathematical models to analyze two types of networks: random networks and scalable networks based on the Barabasi-Albert model. By applying these models, we found specific thresholds at which it becomes beneficial for networks to implement this strategy. For random networks, the critical threshold is directly related to the average degree of its nodes. In contrast, for scale-free networks, this threshold is higher, requiring that the network's power-law exponent be higher than 2 in order for the strategy to be advantageous. We believe that many real-world networks exhibit this feature of scale-free networks, leading to our prediction that adopting this epidemic containment method will typically result in the death of a network's pivotal nodes that keep it connected, ultimately leading to its collapse. This prediction is supported by historical examples, including the destruction of medieval cities and the current impact of COVID-19 on major urban centers. We also discuss the potential for networks to recover from this state of collapse, which we found to be possible through a process we call "renormalization" that alters the distribution of nodes' connections. This process can lead to the formation of more resilient networks, including those based on the Barabasi-Albert model and networks with a mixture of hub and small-cluster nodes. We believe that this process has implications for our understanding of a wide range of phenomena, including the formation of languages, the evolution of cities, and the behavior of financial markets. We end by examining the potential applications of our research to these areas, as well as to the practice of removing isolated nodes from networks as a method of containment. We also explore the related issue of the spread of fires in networks and find that, like epidemics, they can result in the destruction of connected nodes. We believe that this phenomenon has historical parallels, including the burning of the library of Alexandria, and that it can be prevented by promoting diversity in networks. We end by discussing the importance of preserving the connections between nodes that are located on the periphery of networks. We call these nodes "sentinel nodes" and believe that they play a crucial role in maintaining the health and resilience of complex systems. To improve policy optimization, Variance Reduction by Experience Replay (VREE) enhances the existing experience replay technique by modifying the policy objective function to account for the variance of the estimated policy gradients. This approach prevents the policy from overfitting to limited data and induces a connection to the adjusted policy improvement ratio, thereby facilitating more substantial policy updates. In contrast to clipped policy optimization methods, VREE yields a superior policy with significantly reduced computational resources, as demonstrated in multiple challenging domains, including the challenging MuJoCo benchmarks. Our proposed VREE algorithm can be integrated into both natural and policy-aware experience replay settings, resulting in significant improvements over existing methods, according to our comprehensive evaluations. By adjusting the variance threshold, VREE leads to multiple benefits, including increased policy efficiency, enhanced exploration, and the emergence of sparse data collection, as exemplified in a simulated robotics environment. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/VIER.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses

dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with

of the dataset focuses on multiple advanced branching prediction tasks, leveraging
rich dialogue datasets, and applies a variety of structures, including neural 
models. Our newly introduced evaluation metric, expected reciprocal rank, joins 
established metrics in evaluating our models, which demonstrate solid performance 
on anticipated branches, subsequent turns, and continuous conversations. Our best
model achieves an expected reciprocal rank of 20.4 on the MultiTalk Dataset, 
exceeding the performance of rival models, including a 5-turn conversational model. 
Our code and dataset are available at github.com/TowardsZeroPronouns/MultiTalk.

The LHC is poised to explore the fundamentals of QCD through the study of proton-proton collisions at ever-higher energies and luminosities. Proton-proton collisions at the LHC produce a rich variety of subleading contributions, often referred to as'minors,' resulting from sub Processes such as gluon-gluon interactions, heavy quark production, and electroweak boson interactions. These minor processes are consequential, however, because they systematically convey crucial information about the intrinsic properties of protons. This lecture will delve into the intricacies of these minor systems, examining their underlying physics and presenting ongoing and planned experiments at the LHC, including general strategies and selected measurements involving heavy flavors and vector bosons. The discussion will also cover ongoing efforts to integrate data from the LHC and future hadron colliders, leveraging combined capabilities to thoroughly explore the underlying physics of protons. The approach will be illustrated through a discussion of the potential for the HL-LHC and future lepton-proton colliders, such as the Future Circular Hadron Collider and the Compact Linear Collider. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre reveal sources that have remained inactive for an extended period, suggesting they contain neutron stars that have not undergone a recent supernova explosion. A significant fraction of these sources are believed to be binaries involving a neutron star and a star other than a black hole. To explain the sources' inactivity, researchers propose that these neutron stars have a long period of activity, similar to those found in low-mass binary systems observed in the galaxy outside the centre. A long activity period would require a significant delay before the disappearance of the companion star, making it difficult to detect these sources optically. To support this theory, we need to understand how often a particular source becomes active, a metric that can be determined by identifying repeated observations of the same source within the overall X-ray archive. Using a statistical approach, we establish an objective method to define when two observations represent the same source becoming active, and calculate the frequency with which a source becomes active within the observed archive, a measure known as the recurrence period. Based on the available data, we find that the recurrence periods of sources within the Galactic Centre are significantly longer than those outside the centre, a difference so great that it may indicate the sources within the centre have an activity period that will lead to the disappearance of the companion stars, supplementing the previously proposed explanation for their inactivity. Furthermore, we discover that the distribution of recurrence periods is consistent with a exponential distribution, an outcome that can be predicted by modeling the activity periods of these sources. Additionally, we find evidence that the sources within the Galactic Centre have a shorter activity period when the Earth is aligned with the plane of the Galaxy, a effect so substantial that it cannot be attributed to the background radiation alone, suggesting it may be caused by the presence of the Giant Molecular Clouds that lie in the plane of the Galaxy, and that it cannot be explained by the longer activity period proposed previously. Instead, it may be the result of the character of the sources, with those located near the edges of the Galaxy displaying shorter activity periods when the Earth is aligned with the plane of the Galaxy, a phenomenon that persists even when considering only the sources with the longest activity periods outside the centre. Understanding the meaning of diverse phrases with different semantics is a challenging aspect of language interpretation.  This study introduces a novel task called Semantic Variety in Conversation (SVC), where two individuals with different levels of knowledge engage in a conversation about a target statement, and the goal for the second individual is to infer the truth of a target statement based on the conversation.  We demonstrate that SVC outperforms existing tasks in several areas, including natural language inference and conversational knowledge verification.  To accomplish this, we present a system that consists of a teacher that generates conversations and a student that practices inferred truth on the basis of those conversations.  Our results reveal that focusing on semantic variety during conversation generation leads to better outcomes for SVC, NLI, and CONVERSATIONAL-KA.  We hope this research opens up an exciting area of investigation focused on the intricate dynamics of semantic variety in conversation.  To facilitate progress in this region, we are releasing a comprehensive dataset of conversation segments along with code and model weights at https://github.com/nyuVLabs/semantic Variety in Conversation.  This dataset and the SVC task can be adapted to suit a variety of applications and scenarios.  We also present an illustrative example of a conversation about a picture in Figure 1. Massive rotating stars can experience pinching caused by conservation of angular momentum, ultimately leading to massive stars with significant spins. However, the limits of this stability are not well understood, particularly for very low mass stars with convective cores. In this work, a one-dimensional hydrodynamic model of rotating stars was developed to simulate the long-term stability of low mass stars with convective cores by accounting for convective heat transfer, buoyancy caused by rotation, and mass loss. Using this model, we explored the stability of low mass stars with convective cores and found that those with pinched cores are more susceptible to mass loss due to stellar winds and mass loss episodes caused by convective instability beneath the rotating convective core. In fact, these stars are more likely to reach shedding limits below the shedding limits predicted by traditional models, and even above, losing their convective cores and transforming into fully radiative stars. This is particularly true for stars with high spins, and it has significant implications for very low mass stars with convective cores, including brown dwarfs, influencing their final stages of evolution, including the formation of white dwarfs and carbon-oxygen nebulae supernovae. In addition to this, it was found that stars with masses below 2.5 solar masses, including brown dwarfs, experience shedding of their convective cores through an alternative mechanism, driven by high spin energies, and become radiative stars instead. This led to the discovery of a previously unknown branch of low mass stars with radiative cores, and it has significant implications for theories of stellar evolution that aim to better understand the behavior of low mass stars with convective cores and their interactions with the environment. This model was also used to simulate the interaction between convective heat transfer and mass loss, and the resulting shedding limits were found to be lower than predicted limits, and it has significant implications for the decline in mass loss rates observed in stars with convective cores, including low mass stars and brown dwarfs. The method of presenting experimental data with systematics and statistical uncertainties is examined, and a proposed framework is discussed which emphasizes the significance of clear labeling, efficient plot types, and a universal convention for plot elements. The paper emphasizes that researchers' overreliance on figure legends to convey the meaning of measurements, errors, and relevant systematic weights is excessive and may confuse the non-expert. To facilitate interpretation and utilization of experimental data, it is suggested that measurements be displayed as markers on plots, with errors depicted graphically, and that the inclusion of systematic weights as curves on plots be considered. The proposed methods are illustrated with amplitude measurements from particle physics experiments. The paper concludes by suggesting that a permanent repository be created to house code and calibration information essential for interpreting measurement plots. The proposed guidelines are consistent with those found in CERN's ROOT data analysis framework and the EPIC toolkit used by the HepDose package. The framework of the paper is organized to facilitate easy incorporation of its suggestions into existing data analysis codes. The paper concludes by presenting a set of specific figure plotting commands that illustrate the proposed methods with widely used data analysis codes. A new model proposing a self-similar approach to relativistic afterglows, which takes into account the change in observability due to the expansion of the jet, has been developed by its authors in a previous study. This model highlights the transition from narrow to wide jets as a key aspect of its dynamics. In the current research, this model is applied to various jet configurations and observations of gamma-ray bursts. The analysis of these afterglow phenomena reveals that the invariant spectrum remains unchanged across observations, a finding that is further supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, this model predicts specific observed patterns of decreasing brightness with increasing time and frequency. In addition, it is observed that the transition from relativistic to non-relativistic afterglows marks a critical point in time, a point of interest that has been previously noted by other researchers. A key innovation of this model also involves the integration of external energy absorption through shocks, a feature that enhances its analytical capabilities. Furthermore, this model can be integrated with both long and short-duration gamma-ray bursts in a unified afterglow model, a concept that has been proven through observational data. In conclusion, this model has been validated through a comprehensive analysis of observed afterglow phenomena, a result that underscores the self-similar and scaling principles governing these cosmic events. This problem has been proven to be computationally difficult to solve for most graph types. In this research, we established an algorithm that allows for the efficient solution of this problem for a limited number of instances, based on the amount of additional information used in the problem. Specifically, we developed an approach that, given a limited amount of additional information, in a short amount of time accurately determines the maximum number of times a subgraph of two colored vertices can be encountered within the original graph, for a graph of a limited size. In addition, this approach can be used to resolve a related problem of a similar complexity, the maximum subgraph multi-coloring issue. To achieve enhanced stability and energy conservation, we propose a controller that prioritizes high-speed center of mass movement during the straight phase, and favors low-speed movement during the turning phase. To further increase robustness, we have also developed a feedback control system to manage the impact of leg strike. Our simulations have demonstrated the effectiveness of these approaches in realistic scenarios, with the robot successfully navigating uneven terrain and recovering from balance disruptions. Compared to traditional bipedal robots, our propellant-assisted model shows significant improvements in energy consumption and stability in challenging situations. Our findings also highlight the significance of proper valve management in regulating the flow of propellants, and the importance of accurately calibrating sensor readings. Our research has been applied to a real-world demonstration, with a small biobot navigating around obstacles and recovering from falls in a controlled environment. Our results have significant implications for the design of future bipedal robots that utilize internal gases and fluids for movement, with potential applications in space exploration, where weight and energy efficiency are of paramount importance. This property holds in integral domains with a divisorial ideal lattice, specifically those with a compact ideal lattice. A result similar to Gilmer's integral domain characterization is established, yet with an added condition on the set of non-zero divisors. Furthermore, an integral domain with a compact ideal lattice is shown to be a domain with an integral divisor if and only if its prime ideals are divisorial. This implies that domains with a compact ideal lattice are integral domains if and only if they have a one-to-one correspondence between prime and divisorial ideals. This further extends to showing that every domain with an integral divisor is a domain with a one-to-one correspondence between prime and divisorial ideals, thereby being a domain whose ideal lattice is divisorial. This type of valued domain is defined as a valued domain whose value group is divisible and contains no finite subsets, or alternatively, where the set of non-zero values is cohesive and forms a group. In order to make efficient use of power consumption and heat generation in large-scale cloud computing environments, a new approach is proposed that involves decreasing CPU frequencies across all cores by a certain percentage. A simulation was conducted on an actual data center dataset consisting of 200 workloads and spanning various CPU frequencies, and the results showed that reducing frequencies by as little as 20% across all cores can lead to a 10% decrease in overall energy consumption. Furthermore, a comparison was drawn with existing temperature reduction techniques, and the results indicated that decreasing CPU frequencies by a small percentage can also result in a significant decrease in average temperature, which in turn can lead to a 23.2% decrease in processor failure rate. A novel metric called the Energy Temperature Degradation Ratio (ETDR) was introduced to evaluate this kind of frequency-based degradation, and simulation results showed that it varies greatly depending on the data center environment, temperature requirements, and available processing power. Ultimately, the most suitable frequency reduction percentage was determined to be around 30% based on the ETDR calculations, and this kind of degradation was found to be a cost-effective measure that can result in significant energy savings and decreased maintenance costs in cloud computing environments. The proposed technique and the ETDR metric also have applications in fields beyond cloud computing. The simulation code has been made available online for further research and experimentation. The proposed technique and the ETDR metric can be used to explore and evaluate other ways of degrading processors, and a simulation showed that reducing the number of active CPU cores can lead to a 24% decrease in processor failure rate, which in turn results in a 15% decrease in maintenance costs, given that the energy consumption increases by a little over 2%. A localized move called a 2-move is an essential component in welded link theory, qualifying as a move that maintains equivalence in both classical and welded contexts. Our research demonstrates that any classical knot can be transformed into an unknotted state via a sequence of 2-moves, thereby demonstrating the ubiquity of 2-moves in the space of classical knots. Additionally, we establish that the presence of a specific type of loop, known as a grilled loop, in welded links is a decisive criterion, as links containing a grilled loop are necessarily non-welded. Our novel unknotting approach for welded links incorporates both 2-moves and grilled loops, offering a unified procedure that includes the insertion of grilled loops as a key step. This method provides a precise measure of the distance a welded link must be modified to become untangled. Our research further delves into the properties of grilled loops, demonstrating that they possess characteristics similar to the embedded plane properties seen in certain curve monoids. Our novel unknotting procedure for welded links also establishes a connection with the abstract 2-move category, enabling the recovery of the original space of welded links as a sub-space of the 2-move category through a homeomorphism induced by a projection. This projection is achieved by applying the abstraction process to the wired version of an embedded loop, resulting in a loop that can be determined up to 2-move equivalence. This space of welded links is preserved unchanged under the operation of adding a point to the plane, which is equivalent to the behavior seen in the classical context. Our research further elaborates on the properties of grilled loops by examining the effects of the operation of adding a point to the plane on embedded loops, which leads to the discovery of a new type of loop, called a twisted loop. The presence of a loop that is topologically equivalent to a twisted loop in a link dictates that the link is necessarily non-classified, thereby providing a decisive criterion for the distinction between classical and welded link theory. Our novel unknotting procedure for welded links also offers an alternative interpretation based on the concept of 2-move distance, which can be applied to the study of the space of welded links. We've demonstrated that the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space can be represented as a Vassiliev invariant of a specific, elementary knot invariant's origin. Specifically, it arises from the integration of the Fox-Hatcher 1-cocycle, a crucial construct in our proof. This discovery builds on a previous finding by the second author, who showed that this 1-cocycle defines a pure and non-trivial Vassiliev invariant of a higher order. To support this result, we also explore related properties and provide a specific formula for integrating the Fox-Hatcher 1-cocycle along a long knot's space. Additionally, we examine the relation between this construction and a particular variety of composite knots, thereby establishing a connection to the composite knot's space and its associated invariants. This connection can be viewed as a variation of the Vassiliev invariant's properties, which are associated with the variety of composite knots and have been previously established by the first author. We believe that this result may also be a consequence of an even more comprehensive finding, which remains a subject for further investigation. This work was conducted as part of the research project titled: Research on Higher Order Topological Invariants of Knots and Links. The effectiveness of multi-agent collaboration is dependent on the level of integration possible between individual agents, as well as the overall structure of the network in which they operate. This research explores the optimal design of a division of labor in a static, theoretical setting amongst robots with limited computational capabilities, and those that have more advanced capabilities, on a random network. It is assumed that matching is based on a one-to-one correspondence, with the most capable robots being paired with the most advanced computational tasks. The primary goal of this study is to maximize overall system efficiency by optimizing both the level of integration between agents and the structure of the network. It has been mathematically proven that this optimal setting results in a better outcome than a randomly arranged network. Furthermore, this study provides empirical evidence from simulated models, indicating that a more intricate network leads to a higher level of overall system efficiency when there is a limited difference in the level of integration possible between agents. It has also been observed that in cases where there is a significant level of integration possible between agents, an overly complex network can actually decrease overall system efficiency. The findings of this research can be applied to various theoretical settings, including those with various levels of integration possible between agents, those with different network configurations, and those that change over time. The most optimized setting for these settings can be determined using evolutionary algorithms. The effectiveness of these settings has been validated through simulations. This research provides new insights into the optimization of collaborative systems, and provides a platform for further theoretical development, as well as applications in fields such as economics, biology, and sociology. In this work, we introduce a novel concept called Pragmatic Privacy Assaults (PPAs), which involves an attacker participating indirectly in a federated learning process, specifically a vertical collaboration, and then extracting sensitive information from the shared model. Our research involves developing an accurate method to measure PPAs and investigating the effectiveness of PPA attacks in various scenarios. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that attacks are generally less successful when launched by a single attacker but become highly effective with multiple participants collaborating. We also discover that the layer at which the attack is launched has a significant impact on the outcome, with attacks launched on lower layers being more successful. Furthermore, we observe that robust models against PPAs attacks are not significantly more insecure than standard private models. We propose a strategy called PPA-Filter, a simple and efficient approach that enables healthy participants whose data has been compromised to be identified and excluded from the process, thereby enhancing the security of the model with minimal deterioration in its accuracy. Our study on PPA attacks and related issues is now available online. We hope this work will contribute to the development of robust, secure federated learning algorithms capable of withstanding PPA attacks. We intend to extend our research to other learning scenarios affected by similar privacy assaults. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengxiangDrive/PPA. Kernel methods in machine learning, particularly kernel ridge regression, rely heavily on efficient storage and computation with kernel matrices. This research focuses on an interesting aspect of kernel matrix estimation, specifically on the use of random Fourier transformations in noise reduction and kernel estimation. However, the inherent relationship between random Fourier transformation and kernel matrix estimation has not been previously examined in the scientific literature. In order to break new ground, we establish in this paper that there is a direct and equivalent formulation of random Fourier transformation in noise reduction and kernel matrix estimation. This equivalent formulation enables us to derive an optimal threshold for noise reduction and kernel matrix estimation and to develop a method for constructing efficient kernel matrices for new data points. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in noise reduction and kernel matrix estimation, and show that our approach is applicable to various noise reduction methods in the scientific literature. Last but not least, we examine the connection between random Fourier transformation and the Nyström method for kernel matrix estimation, and provide a sample code for noise reduction and kernel matrix estimation by random Fourier transformation. This research was previously unpublished and is now available as a preprint at the arXiv website. The associated code can be found at the GitHub website. In our study, we demonstrated that any group representation can be re-expressed as a combination of subrepresentations involving the wreath products of a group with a permutation group, utilizing a novel Cartesian partition approach. This conversion maintains the original representation's properties, including its irreducibility. We also show that any group representation that cannot be formulated using the wreath product method necessarily possesses a specific, derivable characteristic. Furthermore, we establish that a representation that exhibits certain behavior, such as irreducibility, can be determined to be intrinsic, meaning it is an inherent property of the group itself rather than a result of the representation, by examining the underlying group structure through the lens of its Cartesian partitions. We illustrate our method by applying it to a particular type of representation, known as the regular representation, and also investigate how our approach relates to other established methods of group representation, such as the Frobenius preservation condition and the method of partitioning based on the Schur correspondence. Our findings can be extended to include certain unusual groups, such as nonabelian groups with a single-class representation, and we discuss some open questions regarding these cases. Our research builds upon the foundational work of Ozawa, who demonstrated that any group representation can be re-expressed as the wreath product of a group with a permutation group, although our approach provides a more constructive method for achieving this representation. Our study also establishes a relationship between the group structure and the behavior of its representations, thereby offering a possible route to investigating the intrinsic properties of a group. Our results can be found in the papers titled "Cartesian partitions of groups" and "Irreducible representations of finite groups", both written by us, and also derived from the published research of other mathematicians. To better understand the underlying dynamics of networks, researchers employ various methods to alter network connectivity, including simple addition and removal of nodes and edges. In this study, we introduce a new method of modifying networks by introducing a rule that determines which edge to remove or add based on a threshold value. This result can either lead to the removal of an edge, creating a branch in the network, or the addition of an edge, leading to its destruction. We developed an algorithm to simulate this process on a Cayley tree by adding or removing edges randomly. Our analysis reveals that the distribution of the algorithm's state, known as the N-branching distribution, can be determined through a first-passage time formula. The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is limited by the presence of quadrupolar oscillations in resonant bar detectors, which cause noise spikes and reduce sensitivity. To overcome this limitation, a new detector design is proposed: the sloshing-Sagnak interferometer. This device combines the principles of the Sagnak interferometer with a resonant mass subjected to forced oscillations, allowing for the cancellation of noise spikes through destructive interference. Based on current technology, this proposed design has the potential to enhance the detection of high-frequency signals by improving signal-to-noise ratios and expanding the frequency bandwidth of bar detectors. Specifically, it is anticipated that the sloshing-Sagnak interferometer will be capable of detecting signals with frequencies above 1 kHz, which is currently out of reach for bar detectors. If implemented with the use of advanced materials and optimized resonant masses, this detector could even surpass the sensitivity of laser interferometer detectors at high frequencies, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 per hour for binary neutron star signals with a total mass of 10 Msun. The design of this device also has the potential to be combined with other detection methods, including bar and laser interferometers, to create a network of gravitational wave detectors that can be used to search for gravitational waves across a wide range of frequencies. We explore the underlying causes of NYC's rigidity and examine the effect of a hypothetical earthquake-induced redistribution of mass and charge within the city.  Utilizing satellite imagery, we calculate the total charge distributed across the city, finding it to be primarily concentrated in the financial district of Lower Manhattan.  A significant earthquake in this area could lead to a potentially measurable effect on the behavior of a top-quark pair produced at a nearby particle accelerator, such as those operating at the Large Hadron Collider or a future particle collider built in the area.  However, any cosmic objects with a decay constant less than $10^{24}$ seconds would be unaffected by such a earthquake.  We also consider the implications of injecting antiprotons or heavy quarks into the universe through a cosmic accelerator located in NYC.  In addition, we examine the potential risk of a high-energy particle collision experiment conducted in the city.  For example, a future $100$ TeV particle collider operating in NYC would pose a minuscule risk to the stability of the universe, with the probability of causing a catastrophic universal transformation on the order of $10^{-20}$ per year. This research focuses on creating harmonic modulation techniques that are resistant to changes in their stability, leveraging coupled motional modes in multiple trapped ions. By employing a specific gate design, frequency fluctuations are significantly reduced due to the cancellation of signal effects, resulting in minimal impact on the success rate. Moreover, in cases where mode coupling is significant, this approach yields a more precise achievement of the desired outcome, as the modulation requires an excessive amount of time to cause unintended frequency changes. The frequency instability issue can be illustrated through simulations of both single- and two-ion systems, with experimental implementation feasibility demonstrated for a pair of ions separated by a small distance within a trap. The duration of the gate can be extended to increase resistance to frequency fluctuations, with the potential cost of reduced effectiveness. The potential benefits of this method suggest exploring alternative, potentially more complicated M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate designs that could also be highly resistant to frequency instability. The underlying physics was examined through theoretical analysis, with numerical verification conducted using two- and ten-ion systems. The findings have implications for quantum computing in multiple trapped ion systems, providing a potential solution to the challenge of achieving both low error rates and large scales. We conclude that GaCu$_3$As$_4$ is a unique material worthy of further experimental investigation. We suggest potential markers to look for, including edge states, van Hove singularities, and magnetoelectric effects. This material has a broad range of potential applications, including edge states in (111)-oriented heterostructures and magnetoelectric effects in ferrimagnets. The proposal for the 750 GeV upgrade of the CERN neutrino beam line known as the Beam Dump Experiment (BDE) aims to greatly reduce neutrino flux at the experiment's detection point while increasing the sensitivity to dark sectors. A key aspect of this setup is the nearly collision-free high-energy photon and neutral meson flux at the detection point. The NA62 experiment, operating at the CERN Beam Dump Facility, has an extensive dataset of near-photons and neutral mesons with extensive kinematic information. This leads to an enhanced sensitivity to certain theories such as Massive Neutral Leptons (MNL). In particular, a recent study in the context of the minimal dark photon model highlighted the MNL generation mechanism $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, with a predicted decay length that could be as short as $10^{-12}$ cm, making it challenging to detect. In the present investigation, we explore the prospect of detecting this decay mode within the existing NA62 dataset of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ data, utilizing a specialized selection cut designed to be efficient for this specific process. Furthermore, we investigate the potential of improving the search for MNL within the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay mode at the NA62 experiment with several optimization strategies. In the minimal dark photon model context, we find that the currently available data exhibits a sensitivity to MNL masses as low as $43.5$ MeV, a limit that can be heightened to as low as $47.5$ MeV with a upgraded detector. In addition to this, we investigate the potential of detecting other MNL generation mechanisms such as $K^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ N$, $K^+ \to \pi^0 \tau^+ N$, and $K^+ \to \gamma N$, and analyze the existing dataset's limitations in these cases. Lastly, we estimate the detection capacities of the upgraded NA62 experiment for these decays, finding that it can detect MNL masses as low as $25$ MeV with optimized cut criteria. In the context of the minimal dark photon model, we find that the upgraded NA62 experiment can detect MNL masses as low as $12.5$ GeV with the current detector efficiency, a limit that can be heightened to as low as $13.5$ GeV with a upgraded detector. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on predicting two overlapping faces from a single image, with each predicted face occupying a distinct head pose category. We demonstrate that modeling face overlap is essential and introduce the Self-Aligned Dual Face Prediction Networks (SADRNet) framework, which produces two face configurations in the 3D space with automatically determined orientations. To encourage facial overlap, our model is equipped with a detection module that identifies the most suitable overlap region, and we incorporate a regression layer to guide the face configurations towards a desired alignment. The proposed framework is evaluated through extensive testing on the ATRC-FD dataset, resulting in state-of-the-art performance in average 3D dense alignment error compared to current benchmarks, and also demonstrates superior performance on the AFLW2000-3D dataset in average 3D dense alignment error and reconstruction quality metrics. Moreover, SADRNet is capable of reconstructing complex head orientations and demonstrating robust performance across a range of evaluation metrics. The proposed framework is further applied to train a robust 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction model through self-alignment, which leads to a significant performance boost on unseen data. The code for SADRNet is available at: https://github.com/zhengyangDing/SADRNet.

In an inflationary model, a specific scenario can lead to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs), namely when cosmological perturbations become overly compressed or expanded. We examine the conditions under which this compression or expansion of perturbations can occur in the inflationary period of a particular inflationary model known as $\alpha$-attractor inflation. By analyzing the relationship between initial conditions and the outcome of inflationary perturbations, we determine the press and expansion of perturbations during inflation and after it ends. Compression of perturbations can result in PBH formation, so we establish the minimum amplitude of perturbations required to achieve this compression. We find this minimum amplitude to be directly linked to the specific parameters of the inflationary model and particularly its value of $\alpha$. Consequently, a particular range of values of $\alpha$ can potentially give rise to PBHs. Additionally, we discover that the fraction of PBHs formed also depends on the mass of the horizon during the final stage of inflation and exhibit a non-trivial connection with it. We examine two scenarios, one in which the ending phase of inflation occurs suddenly and another in where it happens gradually, and find that PBH formation is more efficient in the latter case. We also investigate the influence of the inflationary model's specific form on PBH formation and find that a particular characteristic, known as the asymptotic value of the slow-roll parameter, remains constant for all values of $\alpha$ and even extends to the post-inflationary era. Finally, we determine the fraction of PBHs formed per unit range of the inflationary model's specific form and compare it with the overall abundance of PBHs required to explain a particular phenomenon and find that it exceeds it by several orders of magnitude. We conclude by examining potential connections with other inflationary models that share similar characteristics. Lastly, we acknowledge that our findings rely on an analytical approximation of the inflationary perturbations and that further accurate calculations are necessary to validate our results. We also propose that in scenarios in which the ending phase of inflation happens gradually, the formation of PBHs may lead to their distribution being concentrated among the heaviest masses rather than being uniform across all masses. We further suggest that in such cases, further research is needed to determine the exact distribution of these massive PBHs and to investigate the influence of different values of $\alpha$ and the mass of the horizon during the final stage of inflation on this distribution. We intend to undertake these tasks in our forthcoming calculations

We are exploring the concept of "dearest" vertices in ordered and labeled trees, which is a natural extension that incorporates a perceived distance or similarity between letters, likely drawn from a specific subset or overall set of possible characters. A key observation we make about these trees is that there is always at least one vertex that stands out as uniquely distinct from the others - being farther from the root than any other leaf, and in a way that isn't equivalent to the distance between any other pair of leaves. This exceptional vertex we've identified has several important properties, including being located at a maximum depth that is greater than half the total depth of the tree, being situated in a position that isn't mirrored on the other side of the tree, and in general, being farthest from all other leaves in a way that varies depending on the specific ordering of letters. By utilizing a weighted version of this measure, we can weight the significance of each leaf more heavily, which in turn affects the level of depth exhibited by the deepest vertex. The unique properties of this deepest vertex are upheld even in cases where the trees are structured in a way that multiple trees are connected together, as long as these connections occur at the level of individual edges rather than entire branches. The approach we've taken here also extends naturally to weighted trees connected at the branch level, where the highest ranked vertex can be found by examining each branch individually, making it possible to define multiple deepest vertices, one for each branch, by applying the same criteria to each branch separately. The research presented here is an extension of previous work done on ordered and labeled trees, which identified the vertex that was farthest from the root as being critical, and it is our hope that this expanded analysis will provide a more comprehensive understanding of those results. The approach we've taken here is also innovative because it provides a direct and unbiased method for identifying the most significant vertex in each branch of a tree, which in turn makes it possible to apply this approach to problems and scenarios involving fields like linguistics, biology, and cryptography. The paper at large is composed of six sections, including the introduction, the methodology used to define and identify the deepest vertex, the properties of the deepest vertex, the weighted version of this approach, the extension of this method to weighted trees connected at the branch level, and finally a discussion of the research and possible areas for future work. The research presented here has significant implications for fields like linguistics, biology, and cryptography, which could be explored further by combining this approach with methods from fields like machine learning

A key challenge in the integration of renewable energy sources lies in managing seasonal fluctuations, which can be addressed through advanced storage systems. As storage technology improves, there's a growing interest in self-planning energy and storage independently by individual households. Existing research focuses mainly on optimization and storage potential assessment with little consideration of present decentralized energy markets. This study develops a straightforward self-planning method for both energy and storage, taking into account current market practices and pricing mechanisms. By applying this method to real data and scenarios, we find that it leads to conservative storage investment, and that households in colder climates tend to invest more heavily in storage. Furthermore, analysis of market pricing reveals that storage investment is more likely in regions with stable pricing patterns. This study's self-planning method can be implemented with a wide range of tools, making it useful for various contexts beyond decentralized markets. By evaluating different storage investment scenarios, we also demonstrate how this method can be utilized to examine the impacts of various factors on storage investment and decentralized energy production. This study's findings and self-planning method can be applied to other areas, such as smart grids, thermal energy storage, and renewable energy systems, with only minor modifications. This research was conducted without the benefit of machine learning techniques, yet the results show that a simple self-planning method based on linear regression can be highly effective in planning energy and storage independently. This is particularly evident when comparing the differences in storage investment and energy production to the ideal optimization solution. This study's findings suggest that such a self-planning method can be an reliable and cost-effective alternative to optimization algorithms, even with the addition of machine learning elements. This study's data and analysis can be used to evaluate the sustainability of energy and storage planning by individual households, providing a tool for monitoring and assessing this self-planning method, as well as similar methods, in the context of decentralized energy markets. A simplified computer model is used to explore atmospheric circulation on land, without the interference of ocean currents, in various global temperature patterns. This research contrasts atmospheric circulation between two extreme scenarios: a rapidly spinning atmosphere seen in tropical regions and a slowly spinning atmosphere prevalent in mid-latitude areas. By analyzing various pressure gradients and wind speeds in computer-simulated environments, a range of circulation patterns emerges, branching into two distinct categories. One group, characterized by extremely fast wind speeds in high-altitude atmospheres, is associated with super-rotation, similar to that observed in some planetary bodies. Another group, marked by wind speeds that change more gradually with altitude, exhibits geostrophic turbulence, similar to patterns found in mid-latitude areas on Earth. The division between these two groups is marked by a critical point where the rotation speed of the system reaches a certain level in relation to its atmospheric height. Below this threshold, geostrophic turbulence dominates, while above it, super-rotation and turbulent turbulence coexist in a stable equilibrium. This relationship is highly sensitive to changes in global temperature patterns and affects wind speeds and circulation patterns significantly. The interaction between these patterns also creates unique precipitation patterns and areas of low pressure that resemble the areas where precipitation and low pressure generally occur in Earth's mid-latitude areas. The computer model used in this research allows for the direct calculation of precipitation and low-pressure areas from the computer-simulated data, which matches the patterns observed in Earth's mid-latitude areas. The coexistence of super-rotation and turbulent turbulence, coupled with their effects on precipitation and low-pressure areas, have been documented in a stable equilibrium state for the first time in the available scientific literature. The reduction of the computer model used in this research enables the calculation of precipitation and low-pressure areas that occur in Earth's mid-latitude areas through the direct integration of atmospheric circulation patterns, which has not been achieved through any other method in the available scientific literature. The computer model used in this research can be applied to other planetary bodies that have atmospheric circulation on land, without the interference of ocean currents, in various global temperature patterns. The findings of this research have important implications for the understanding of atmospheric circulation on land in various global temperature patterns and provide a new perspective on the processes that lead to the formation of precipitation and low-pressure areas in these patterns. This work delves into the underlying causes for the limitations of massive batch training. To overcome these constraints, the authors develop an alternative strategy. They demonstrate that, by alternating between smaller batches for efficient training and larger batches for data enrichment, they can achieve comparable performance to dedicated semi-supervised learning techniques while reducing labeling costs. The authors further expand upon this approach in a pivotal experiment, combining big batches with careful model fine-tuning, and successfully apply it to real-world images. The resulting method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques by a 1% margin on CIFAR-100 and matches the performance of semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. The code is available at github.com/DeepLearningAssistanceGroup/dynamic-learning.

In this work, we provide a graduated transformation construction methods 
for Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs), demonstrating that HNNs are capable of 
encompassing gradient-based updates within their dynamics. We also offer a 
numerical example highlighting the capability of HNNs to capture the dynamics 
of a simple pendulum using the Cart-Pole model, as well as the Cart-Pendulum 
model itself. Furthermore, we show that HNNs can produce control signals for 
the Cart-Pendulum model when the system reaches a unstable equilibrium point, 
demonstrating the system's ability to move towards a stable state. Additionally, 
we explore the relationship between HNNs and Energy-Shaped controllers, revealing 
that both control methods yield identical dynamics when the system is linear. 
In the linear case, we also demonstrate that HNNs are capable of determining 
the system's state from the output, thereby enabling the derivation of state 
estimation filters. We conclude by examining the potential implications of HNNs 
for understanding the connections between recurrent neural networks, control systems, 
and Hamiltonian systems, as well as exploring future research directions such 
as the analysis of HNN stability or the creation of learning algorithms for 
HNNs. Lastly, we provide the MATLAB code for the simulations presented in the 
paper at this link: https://github.com/amin-chakmakhanian/HNN-Gradients.
