Recent advances in large language models have achieved high performance on numerous natural language processing tasks, outperforming traditional machine learning methods. However, these models require significant computational resources for training and significant amounts of data for effective utilization. To bridge this gap, this work presents a new framework called Ability that leverages existing models and knowledge structures to train and fine-tune large language models efficiently. Ability enables the integration of external knowledge into language models through structured resources, such as knowledge graphs and lexical databases, without necessitating vast amounts of labeled data for model training. Instead, it allows for targeted incorporation of knowledge by mapping model outputs to desired properties, effectively enabling controlled exploration of the model's knowledge. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework in both training and inference tasks, and show that it facilitates seamless integration of external knowledge with low computational expense. Furthermore, we explore various strategies for knowledge integration and analyze the trade-offs between them. Overall, this work provides a versatile platform for incorporating structured knowledge into large language models, thereby expanding their capabilities to a broader range of tasks. Code available at: https://github.com/ghrua/Ability.

High-resolution vector maps are gaining popularity, and their need for precise geometric representations is resulting in the use case for raster map sources being reinterpreted. A significant drawback of using these sources is the presence of aliasing artifacts, particularly with line junctions, which significantly disrupt the visual experience. In contrast to existing anti-aliasing techniques that are optimized for raster maps, this research introduces an efficient method for rendering line junctions when using vector maps. By utilizing a straightforward yet effective technique based on bezier curve analysis, this approach provides a high-level abstraction that allows for easy implementation across different vector map platforms. A comparison with popular raster map sources demonstrates that this method effectively mitigates aliasing issues with line junctions, even when using low-resolution raster maps. A lightweight JavaScript implementation of this technique is made available as an open-source contribution. By applying this method to your applications, you can eliminate line junction aliasing and significantly enhance the visual quality of your maps. The code can be found at https://github.com/mapbox/junction-anti-alias. The documentation for using the API is available at https://docs.mapbox.com/mapboxing.js/api/#JunctionAntiAliasing. The resolution this method provides can range from 1dpix to 4dpix, which correlates to the following vector map specifications: - 1dpix: 1536x1536 - 2dpix: 768x768 - 3dpix: 512x512 - 4dpix: 256x256. In recent years, multi-channel speech processing has gained significant attention, and techniques such as differential microphones have been widely used in various applications. However, when one or more microphone channels are affected by noise, it is challenging to enhance the corresponding individual channels. To address this difficulty, this paper proposes a new dual-path model, the DPCRN network, which simultaneously generates and estimates the clean and noisy individual channels. By exchanging these estimated channels, the DPCRN network achieves better performance in cleaning the noisier channels. Experimental evaluations conducted under a range of conditions show that the proposed DPCRN network delivers superior performance compared to leading baselines, with the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement ranging from 1.5 to 4.5 dB depending on the scenario. Moreover, the proposed model demonstrates its versatility by integrating seamlessly into existing multi-channel speech separation frameworks, thereby setting a high standard for future individual channel speech improvement techniques. The associated code and models are available for public use at: https://github.com/ASRGroup/DPCRN.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modeling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. Nonetheless, a persistent and considerable error is observed in relation to direct numerical simulation references figures for the overall circulation height and temperature gradient. The model in question also exhibits a relatively short warm layer regime in comparison to its direct numerical simulation counterpart. The underlying issue is determined to stem from the inadequate treatment of boundary conditions rather than the two-fluid model itself. The paper concludes by highlighting the potential of this approach for modeling atmospheric convection, with suggested areas for future enhancement including the integration of boundary condition treatment and sub-filter variation modeling. The accompanying code is available online for public use. The underlying numerical techniques including the time-stepping method, the spatial discretization method, and the boundary condition treatment method are discussed in detail. The present two-fluid model shares some similarities with the 2007 model developed by Valcke, with the key distinction lying in the time-stepping method used. The paper also compares its own results with the aforementioned 2007 model of Valcke, with the resulting differences attributed to the time-stepping method used in the present model. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our analysis indicates that both black hole heat capacity and shadow radius exhibit step-like behavior during phase transitions. We also find that the shadow radius can serve as a probe for revealing the thermal profile of black holes in the context of the EPYM gravity framework. Our research can be applied to various situations, including quantum gravity, condensed matter physics, and astrophysics, where non-linear black hole interactions occur. We further propose that future observations of black hole shadows can provide insights into the non-linear gravity environment and the matter that gives rise to it. We also analyze the relationship between shadow radius and horizon radius in the context of a nonlinear charged AdS black hole within the Einstein-Yang-Mills (EYM) gravity framework as a comparison to the EPYM gravity framework. This comparison reveals that the EYM and EPYM gravity frameworks exhibit distinct differences in their thermal behavior and shadow radius thermal phase transition in the context of the big small black hole coexistence phases. These differences arise due to the difference in the number of nonlinear field interactions in the EYM and EPYM gravity frameworks. We propose that future observations of black hole shadows in the context of the EYM and EPYM gravity frameworks will provide insights into the non-linear gravity environment and the field interactions that give rise to it. Recently, a new medium called 360-degree virtual travel video has gained popularity, allowing for immersive and engaging experiences. To create more realistic and interactive 360-video content, researchers are exploring automated methods for generating predictive user actions. One such approach involves viewport forecasting, which estimates the future screen location based on captions in videos. Although this technique has been successful for standard video formats, there is no existing knowledge on how to apply it to 360-degree virtual travel videos. This study builds upon existing caption-based viewport forecasting methods and adapts them to predict user views in 360-degree videos. By utilizing a sub-network focused on caption analysis, this method demonstrates comparable performance to existing techniques on standard video datasets and showcases the potential for 360-degree video forecasting. Moreover, this research presents a novel application for caption-based viewport forecasting in 360-degree videos, offering a feasible solution for various 360-degree content creation tasks. To facilitate future research and development in this area, the authors publicly release a 360-degree viewport forecasting dataset, along with a 360-degree video captioning model. This work presents a groundbreaking approach that paves the way for utilizing viewport forecasting in 360-degree content creation, enhancement, and optimization for various purposes. We provide a new approach to developing a priori error estimates for a wide range of time-dependent partial differential equations with restricted effectiveness. These equations have conserved quantities that maintain stability and Dirac delta initial data. We achieve our results by employing scale-based approximations, decoupling techniques, and the theory of wave equations with restricted effectiveness. This method yields error bounds that account for the inaccuracies introduced by the scale-based approximations and the inherent limitations of the efficacy of the equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our error estimates to specific models, such as the Boltzmann equation and the Stokes system, which have not been previously analyzed using a priori methods. The error estimates for these models take the form of $|u_k|_{L^2} \leq C \left(\sqrt{\lambda_k} + \sqrt{\epsilon} \sqrt{\lambda_k}^{1/4} e^{-c\sqrt{\lambda_k}/(2\sqrt{\epsilon})}\right)$, where $\epsilon$ is the efficacy parameter and $\lambda_k$ is the $kth$ Dirac sequence eigenvalue. This result takes the form of a Gevrey class with index $1/2$ when the efficacy is slightly reduced, which implies that the solutions to these equations possess a regularizing effect that classifies them as Shillings-type equations. This further extends to generalized Stokes and Boltzmann equations, which also fall under this category. Finally, we offer a summary of the main developments and outline a strategy for extending the results to other time-dependent partial differential equations with restricted effectiveness. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution, denoted as $G_{TMD}(x)$, is examined. This function, integral in form, involves a non-trivial integration that exposes $G_{TMD}(x)$ to infrared renormalons, initially undetected in prior studies. Utilizing the gauge invariant integral technique, the presence of these renormalons is confirmed and their impact on the TMD distribution is demonstrated. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the average value of $G_{TMD}(x)$ is systematically overestimated by a factor of two, with the underlying physical explanation related to the small-$x$ behavior influenced by infrared renormalons. This finding also implies that the ratio of the average to the maximum possible value of $G_{TMD}(x)$ is approximately 2.5. Hikishima et al. previously found a similar ratio for the colorm dipole gluon distribution function within the small-$x$ regime, although their analysis was integral in form and thus insensitive to infrared renormalons. This similarity between the two approaches suggests that the $x$ dependence of $G_{TMD}(x)$ or the corresponding function integral is consistent with the same power law behavior, with exponents equal to $2$ and $3$ respectively. This shared behavior among the two approaches aids in better understanding the complex small-$x$ structure of $G_{TMD}(x)$ and the associated dipole matrix element. This result is relevant to quark and gluon distribution functions within the small-$x$ range and can be verified through data from deep inelastic scattering experiments or proton-proton collisions at high energy, such as those obtained from the LHC or the Future Electron-Proton Collider. Many real-world situations involving knowledge transfer can be represented by decisions made under limited information. This paper addresses the challenge of initiating learning for new classes without prior data, a fundamental issue in decision-based black-box transfer. A key contribution here is a systematic analysis of decision-based black-box learning, revealing that it essentially involves making predictions based on partial knowledge about the input distribution. To overcome the obstacle of having no training data for new classes, we develop a method that leverages the structure of decision-based black-box learning to facilitate transfer by learning the conditional distribution of inputs given output decisions, effectively enabling predictive models to be trained for new classes without additional data. This approach is applicable to a wide range of black-box models and is particularly beneficial for models where the output space is small or discrete. Experimental results on various black-box models demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and we also analyze the impact of different factors on knowledge transfer in decision-based black-box learning. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang-nus/zero-shot-dbbtf.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a module that has no repeated composition factors is relatively straightforward, given its full factorization structure. However, for a module with repeated composition factors, building its submodule lattice is more complex, depending on the structure of its factorization and the lattice of its submodules. In this paper, we outline approaches to reconstructing the lattice of submodules of a module with repeated composition factors, drawing on and extending the methods developed for module lattice construction from exchange graphs, as well as on its relationship to the lattice itself. We demonstrate these general approaches using specific modules, including a module whose submodules form a known lattice, allowing for the method's validity to be verified. We also explore modules with composition factor structures similar to that of the partition lattice, providing insights into the approach's potential for applying to other modules. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the exponents of a module's composition factors and the number of submodules one module contains relative to another, enabling this number to be determined for modules with isomorphic composition factor structures. We conclude by examining modules with distinct composition factor structures and demonstrate how these modules contain every lattice that can be formed from a subset of their composition factors, implying they have a universal nature. We also explore the relationship between these modules and the finite lattices that can be formed from the subset of their composition factors, demonstrating that they have a modular structure and identifying their submodules. We end by identifying some open questions related to these modules. The paper's methods for building module lattice structures are geared towards the mathematician specializing in module lattice construction, while its results on lattice and module properties are geared towards the algebraic researcher interested in modules, lattice theory, and algebra. The paper's content is also accessible to the graduate student in mathematics interested in module lattice construction, algebra, and lattice theory. The paper contains nine figures and tables illustrating the module and lattice structures discussed in the text. The paper ends with a list of problems related to the module and lattice structures discussed in the text. Tuning the hyperparameters of reinforcement learning (RL) methods to train neural machine translation models on large datasets is a time-consuming process. To accelerate this process, we propose a method called Proportional Learning Without Exploration (PLWE) in which a single hyperparameter is consistently raised or lowered based on the change in the target metric, until the desired metric is achieved. We also introduce a weighted version of our method to handle multiple objectives, demonstrating its effectiveness in both individual and combined tasks. Our proposed technique consistently outperforms a range of competing RL methods when hyperparameters are left unoptimized, and our results show a significant improvement over the baseline approach. Specifically, our method delivers notable gains of 1.58 and 1.25 when evaluated on the WMT English-to-German and Finnish-to-English translation tasks respectively. Our proposed action transformation technique provides a steady path towards converged results without experiencing the common issue of action space expansion, and our data-driven approach to determine optimal action transformation proportions delivers a boost of up to 1.93 when evaluated on the WMT English-to-German translation task. Our method is suitable for hyperparameter tuning within the realm of RL for neural machine translation, and our results demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing the existing baseline results by a margin of up to 2.08 when evaluated on a range of translation tasks. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/proportional-learning-without-exploration.

We explore how the repetitive operator σ2, which generates a sequence of operators, affects biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space. By analyzing the effects of σ2 on biharmonic hypersurfaces, we establish that a hypersurface is biharmonic if it satisfies specific curvature conditions and is invariant under the operator σ2. Additionally, we establish that an isoparametric hypersurface is biharmonic if it is invariant under the operator σ2, without requiring it to be irreducible. Furthermore, we provide examples and counterexamples to demonstrate the necessity of the operator σ2 in these cases. By comparing these results with earlier research, we also discuss the implications for the fundamental theorem of biharmonic hypersurfaces. Lastly, we offer a conclusion and some open questions regarding the operator σ2 and biharmonic hypersurfaces.

Given any real number p greater than 1 and any integer q greater than 1, this paper defines a new notion called p/q-identifiable sets within the context of number theory, specifically within the realm of integer arrays and quadratic forms. It then demonstrates the connection between these sets and a prominent Diophantine equation, as well as establishes criteria for any subset of the natural numbers to be considered p/q-identifiable. Furthermore, it proves a p/q-identifiable set will necessarily have a specific distributional characteristic, mirroring a consequence initially discovered by the Polish mathematician Sierpiński for a different class of numbers. Additionally, it demonstrates that certain well-known classes of numbers are p/q-identifiable, yet not (1+sqrt(5))/2-identifiable. Lastly, it shows any subset of the natural numbers that is distributed in a particular random manner is not p/q-identifiable, thereby establishing a distinction between deterministic and random number arrays. This work was presented initially at the 2010 Combinatorics and Number Theory Conference held in Budapest.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained
significant popularity in recent years. Despite its success, MongoDB's
transactional functionality remains understudied in the database research
community. This paper addresses this gap by delving into the validation of
MongoDB's transactional integrity in its latest version, version 5.0. We
outline the core features of MongoDB transactions, followed by a comprehensive
 examination of how MongoDB ensures the consistency of its data through
transactional mechanisms. We then survey existing research on MongoDB's
transactional layer, focusing on validation approaches and our own method.
Our transaction validation method involves verifying the correctness of
MongoDB's transactional layer by comparing the database's state before and
after completing a transaction. We validate the integrity of MongoDB's
transactions using a customized version of the TPC-C benchmark and our own
specifications, both of which yield consistent results. Our findings suggest
that MongoDB's transactional integrity can be assured through validation
using our method, which we demonstrate using TPC-C and custom specifications
based on previous research. We also explore the performance costs of
MongoDB's transactional features and offer recommendations for their optimization. Lastly, we acknowledge the rising importance of distributed MongoDB
transactions and identify research opportunities in this area. Our code and
benchmarks are available online at https://github.com/validates/validate-mongodb.

Using the elementary symmetric polynomial basis, we show the positivity of a specific set of coefficients from a new perspective. Specifically, we prove the positivity of coefficients associated with chromatic symmetric polynomials, expressed as exponential sums of elementary symmetric polynomials, via an analysis of the inverse Kostka matrix. This investigation builds on a related finding concerning the positivity of coefficients in a different polynomial context. Furthermore, our investigation implies the positivity of a specific subset of chromatic symmetric polynomial coefficients, which extends a prior result of Kyardsky and the first author. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this approach to a broader class of polynomials, including, for example, the structured Hilbert polynomials, thus demonstrating the utility of this method as a tool for investigating the positivity of various parameter configurations. This research was motivated by a prior result of the first author and Kyardsky, who established the positivity of the coefficients associated with the number of involutions under the elementary symmetric polynomial basis. The positivity of the inverse Kostka matrix has been previously demonstrated by the first author, which is a different context. On the other hand, the positivity of the coefficients associated with the structured Hilbert polynomials can be compared with the results obtained using the monomial symmetric polynomial basis, which yields different and additional insights into the configuration stability of these polynomials. Contrary to expectations, the reduction in solar wind pressure gradient did not result in higher electron energy measurements as would be predicted by the conservation of solar breeze momentum. This discrepancy persists throughout the 180 million kilometer radius range observed and highlights the role of magnetic convergence within the inner heliosphere as a governing factor over fast solar wind decay. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the degree of magnetic convergence plays a more significant part in determining energy levels than does the degree of solar wind speed variation. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. The findings can be applied to a wide range of real-world problems, including smart grids and supply chains, where the presence of malicious actors could have severe consequences. The research also uncovers interesting insights into the trade-off between compression and trustworthiness in the context of robust optimization. The proposed algorithm has been shown to be adaptable to dynamic environments, where the set of trustworthy agents can change over time. The study also delves into the energy efficiency of the proposed algorithm, emphasizing the critical role of node degree in the graph constructed through communication between agents. The research has been published in the journal IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics, Volume 16, Issue 1, January 2020. Our analysis focuses on the BART model, which we challenge to produce grammatically correct and logically consistent sentences from given word sequences. We investigate five scenarios by asking BART to arrange five different sets of words, including phrases with simple syntax and semantics similar to those found in children's books. Our findings reveal that BART successfully generates sentences with correct word orders and captures the underlying meanings of the input words. However, our results also indicate that BART struggles with more complex scenarios, such as arranging words with ambiguous meanings and phrases containing relative pronouns. We believe that understanding how well these models perform in word arrangement tasks can provide valuable insights into their ability to grasp language structure and semantics. Our work utilizes the BART model but our approach can be applied to other similar models. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n$ and its subfields $K_1, \ldots, K_n-1$. Define the function $\mu_{K_1,\ldots, K_n-1}(x)$ as the minimum of the norms of elements in $K$ with ranks 1 through $n-1$ relative to the bases provided by $K_1,\ldots, K_n-1$. For a given field $K$ with a specific property of being minimal, the function $\mu_K(x)$ represents the minimum norm of an element with rank 1 in $K$. Using the approach of [5], our research utilizes the concept of successful minima to establish the relationship between $\mu_K(x)$ and $\mu_{K_1,\ldldots, K_n-1}(x)$. This relationship is expressed as the inequality $\mu_K(\gamma x)^{1/n} \leq \mu_{K_1,\ldots, K_n-1}(\gamma x)$ holding true for all positive real numbers $\gamma$ and $x$. A similar concept of successive minima exists for curves over global fields, where the function $\mu_{\infty}$ determines the minimum norm of a point on the curve with rank 1, and the function $\mu_2$ determines the minimum of the squares of the coordinates of a point on the curve with rank 2. The main theorem established in this paper for number fields is the relationship $\mu_K(\gamma x)^{1/n} \leq \mu_{K_1,\ldots, K_n-1}(\gamma x)$ holding true for all positive real numbers $\gamma$ and $x$, which further implies the inequality $\mu_K(x) \leq \Delta_{n-1} \cdots \Delta_1 \cdot \Delta_K \cdot x^{2(n-1)/n}$. The main theorem established in this paper for curves over global fields is the relationship $\mu_{\infty}(\gamma x) \leq \mu_2(\gamma x)$ holding true for all positive real numbers $\gamma$ and $x$, which further implies the inequality $\mu_{\infty}(x) \leq \Delta_2 \cdot \Delta_{\infty} \cdot x^4$. The second result can be applied to establish the non-rationality of a number field or the absence of rational points on a curve

We introduce a new framework where cluster algebras are integrated into geometric terms, specifically within the context of projective lines and their extensions to flag varieties. We demonstrate how this integration leads to a characterization of the cluster structure associated with the Lusztig quantum group $\mathbb{C}_q(G)$ through the use of $\mathbb{Z}$-orbit forms. As a result, we derive an explicit description of the $\mathbb{Z}$-structure associated with quantum clusters, together with a demonstration that this structure is associated with the Weyl group transformations on $\mathbb{Z}$-forms. Furthermore, we establish that the $\mathbb{Z}$-orbit structure of $G$ is directly related to the folding of the diagram resulting from the extension of the projective line from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}^r$. Alongside generalizations to derived representations and tori, our findings also imply that the cluster structure of the Laumon-Mukai matrix is an exceptional case that cannot be extended to more general Langlands parameters. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with a public transaction record that allows us to map its structure using network analysis tools. By utilizing Ethereum's transaction data and a custom-made data processing approach, we were able to create a detailed representation of the scheme's intricate layout. In a breakthrough, our findings reveal a distinctive pattern of interconnected triangles in each tier of the network, a previously unknown element of pyramid scams. Furthermore, we discover a distinctive difference between standard multi-level marketing businesses and pyramid scams, offering a theoretical contribution to the existing Scam Diagram. Moreover, in a real-world application, we develop a practical solution to filter out scam participants, thereby identifying a subset of the most crucial participants that could be useful for business analysis. Lastly, by examining the ethical implications of building blockchains on transparent networks, we pose a set of research questions that encourage further investigation into the intricacies of decentralized Scams. The data and research methods used in this study are now available as an open-source repository for the academic community to build upon in the next section.

In this work, we introduce a new clustering method called Influence Driven Structure Learning or IDS Learning for complex systems like networks and time series data. These systems comprise interconnected components that affect and are affected by each other. The goal of IDS Learning is to group system components based on their influence on each other, categorizing them as influencers, that are followed by others, or isolates, not followed by any other component. The challenge lies in identifying relationships and determining the direction of their impact. Therefore, we utilize IDS Learning to create networks and time series models where the structure and dynamics can be represented by nonlinear equations. The algorithm itself involves using a combination of optimization and sampling techniques to discover the shape and characteristics of the surfaces that define these systems' behaviors. Furthermore, IDS Learning provides a 2D projection of network graphs and time series models, offering a visual representation of its clustered structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to randomly generated systems and more practically, to real-world data consisting of satellite images and functional magnetic resonance data. These examples show that IDS Learning is capable of accurately and consistently reconstructing complex systems and uncovering their hidden patterns. The code for IDS Learning is available at https://github.com/ashrafmon/IDS Learning. The underlying problem of IDS Learning can be formulated as an instance of a more general problem known as a multi-objective surface fitting challenge. The code for the challenge's solver is also available at https://github.com/ashrafmon/MOSFC. The term 'influence' in IDS Learning refers to the impact one system component has on another, different from the term 'influence' used in other contexts like machine learning. We use IDS Learning to group satellite images' features based on their spatial frequency, resulting in a clustering that aligns with the existing scale-space theory. We use IDS Learning to group functional magnetic resonance data's regions based on their connectivity, resulting in a clustering that aligns with the existing integration information theory. We believe that IDS Learning's unique method of discovering the shape of the surfaces that define complex systems' behaviors and dynamics can be applied to other contexts like security and finance. The challenge of IDS Learning is related to but differs from the challenge of multi-objective optimization, the challenge of surface fitting, and the challenge of clustering. The code for the challenge of multi-objective optimization is available at https://github.com/ashrafmon/MOCO. The code for the challenge of surface fitting is available at https://github.com/ashrafmon/MSFC

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) rely on two interconnected components: a generator creating fake data resembling the target distribution and a discriminator differentiating real data from fabricated information. In standard GAN training, both the generator and discriminator are equally developed through simultaneous training, which can result in unstable convergence and poor performance. We introduce SparseGAN, a novel GAN framework featuring asynchronous training between a versatile generator and a pair of sparse linear discriminators. We leverage the benefits of internal antagonism by combining the individual assessments of multiple discriminators, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our models. We empirically verify that SparseGAN outperforms basic GAN models on various tasks, including image and text generation. Specifically, our text creation model achieves superior results on text-to-text transformation and generating long-form texts according to a given summary. We also successfully apply SparseGAN to complex text datasets such as long-form books and movie scripts. Code is available at: https://github.com/yashSodhi/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of determining whether this theory is true or not. To tackle this issue, researchers propose using genetic data from extraterrestrial sources, perhaps obtained through sample return missions, to determine whether microorganisms that travel through space could have originated from another planetary system. However, creating a statistical test that can identify the presence of interstellar panspermia is complicated by several factors, including the limited amount of genetic information available, the influence of cosmic radiation, and the uncertainty surrounding the duration of time microorganisms can survive in space. In this paper, different models of genetic survival are examined and it is shown that, although the statistics appear unfavourable at first glance, they hide a key insight - the simplest model that could potentially fit the data actually performs poorly. To improve the results, more sophisticated models of genetic survival are considered, including ones that account for the effects of cosmic radiation and the variability of survival times. When these more advanced models are applied to hypothetical sample return missions, it becomes clear that obtaining a viable genetic sample large enough to support the idea of interstellar panspermia would be extremely challenging, if not impossible, given the current understanding of astrophysical contexts. For instance, even a large enough genetic sample weighing a gram would likely fail to reach a probability of interstellar origins greater than 99% with current technology, mainly due to the limited amount of genetic variation it would contain. Therefore, detecting the presence of interstellar panspermia through genetic analysis alone is very difficult, if not impractical, and it would be more effective to look for physical evidence of microorganisms that travel through space. In the case of Earth, analyzing genetic data from meteorites that contain organic matter could provide some insight into the possibility of interstellar panspermia, but it would require developing a more precise method of analysing meteorite samples. In the context of sample return missions, it is recommended to obtain physical samples of microorganisms rather than relying on genetic analysis, and to consider searching for signs of past life that could have survived the journey through space. Animal population studies often rely on capture-recapture data, which involves capturing and identifying individual animals within a defined area, and combining this information with historical location data from selected sites by individual animals. By combining these sources of data, researchers can accurately estimate the size and density of animal populations. However, capture-recapture data are often collected in areas with well-defined boundaries, limiting the accuracy of population estimates. A new method incorporates capture-recapture data collected within enclosed areas with corresponding selected site data from the same area to provide more reliable population density estimates. Furthermore, this method facilitates inferences about area use and population size from capture-recapture data, without constraining the studied area's shape or size. It also accounts for detection biases and provides Bayesian estimates of population density based on capture-recapture data, selected site data, and the area's physical characteristics. In a study on black bear populations, this method yielded superior estimates compared to conventional capture-recapture methods, and demonstrated how capture-recapture data can be used to investigate site fidelity, age-related effects on area use, and the effectiveness of conservation efforts. The method has been implemented in the R package RMark, and can be applied to various animal species, including bears, deer, and fish. The R package SCRrepo also provides models for estimating birth rates and mortality rates based on capture-recapture data, selected site data, and the area's physical characteristics. The R code for models and data analysis is available upon request. The method has been successfully tested on real data and facilitates accessible population analysis, available online. The method has been named Combined Analysis of Capture-recapture and Resource Selection, or CARS. The CARS method differs from conventional capture-recapture analysis by incorporating selected site data from the same area as capture-recapture data, which provides more accurate population estimates, and offers novel research opportunities on area use, site fidelity, and conservation efforts. The method has been validated through simulations and on real data of black bear populations, and demonstrates its effectiveness in combining capture-recapture data and selected site data from the same area with physical characteristics, which enables inferences about area use, site fidelity, and population size, and provides Bayesian estimates of population density based on capture-recapture data, selected site data, and the area's physical characteristics. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a higher level of accuracy than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the transmission of solutions within multilayer networks composed of identically structured layers. By applying this approach to multilayer networks, we can establish conditions under which signals can be transmitted between layers, specifically in regards to the Kuramoto model. By analyzing a model with two layers, we demonstrate the transmission of dynamics from one layer to the other. Furthermore, we show that layers with different rotation speeds can also exchange signals, thereby affecting the nodes' rotation speeds. Ultimately, our findings on a double-layer network can be generalized to complex multilayer networks with many layers, each composed of numerous connected elements. The method we've introduced provides a means of investigating the transmission of signals within these complex networks, although the specific conditions of signal transmission remain an open question requiring further investigation. Given a field $K$ containing a finite subset $S$ as its subfield, and a quadratic extension $L$ of $K$ with the basis $\{1,\tau\}$, we define the set $V_S(\tau)$ as the collection of vectors formed by elements of $L$ with coefficients from $S$. A specific transformation group $G_\tau(S)$ acts on $V_S(\tau)$, and our study focuses on identifying the orbits of this action for various $\tau$ values. When $L$ is a Gaussian extension over $K$, we demonstrate that the action results in distinct orbits for all $\tau$ values, including non-rational ones. Additionally, our analysis leads to a characterization of the parameter $\tau$ as it defines the Gaussian extensions equivalent to $L$. Furthermore, our approach enables us to investigate the distribution of vector trajectories for a given $\tau$, and we establish that only rational $\tau$ values produce periodic trajectories, whereas the geometric trajectories are found for non-rational $\tau$ values. Lastly, our work also examines the algebraic properties of $\tau$ values, establishing that the orbital spaces are distinct under the action of $G_\tau(S)$ for non-equivalent Gaussian extensions, and demonstrating that the parameter $\tau$ defines these extensions uniquely. Our study further explores the connection between the geometric trajectories and the algebraic properties of $\tau$, and we show that the geometric trajectories arise from the action of $G_\tau(S)$ on the set $V_S(\tau)$ for non-rational $\tau$ values, and these trajectories are distinct for all non-rational $\tau$ values. Our results also generalize to the case of finite extensions rather than Gaussian extensions. Our approach utilizes the concepts from field theory and the properties of elements within a field, and it provides an alternative to the approach based on the Galois theory. Our work further leads to the investigation of the distribution of vector trajectories, and it results in a characterization of the parameter $\tau$ as it defines the finite extensions over $K$. Our study also examines the distribution of vector trajectories for a given $\tau$, and it enables the classification of $\tau$ values based on the structure of the corresponding finite extensions. Our results further demonstrate that only rational $\tau$ values produce periodic trajectories, and our study also examines the connection between the geometric trajectories and the algebraic properties of $\tau$ values, and it results in the characterization of the parameter $\tau$ as it defines the finite extensions over $K$.

We examine the challenge of developing accurate representations of large networks from limited local views in the presence of malicious nodes. In a model where nodes have limited communication capabilities and the network adheres to a specific small-world structure, we investigate the difficulties associated with precise network size estimation. Our key discovery indicates that, despite the presence of malicious nodes, a node can still accurately estimate the network's size by employing a specific estimation approach that relies on the gradual reduction of incorrect data due to the robust nature of the small-world model. Our research also delves into the challenging scenario of network size estimation, incorporating the influence of malicious nodes on distance measurements. Our proposed algorithm enables a node to track and discard unreliable distance measurements, thereby reducing the impact of malicious nodes on estimation accuracy. Our theoretical analysis, combined with simulation results, demonstrates the effectiveness of our approaches in networks with both homogeneous and heterogeneous node connections. Our findings further illustrate that in highly dispersed networks, the presence of malicious nodes has minimal impact on the accuracy of size estimation. Our research offers novel insights into the interplay between the presence of malicious nodes and network centrality, as well as the difficulties associated with estimating network sizes in small-world graphs. Our work also paves the way for further exploration into the influence of malicious nodes on other network estimation tasks. Our simulation code is available at https://github.com/linga110/ScaleEstimation. Our research received funding from the Australian Research Council. Detecting and managing traffic congestion rely heavily on accurate traffic state estimates, particularly queue lengths. This study introduces a novel approach to estimate short-term queue sizes without assuming queue lengths remain stable or using traffic models. A combinatorial method is created to estimate queue sizes based on the trajectories of free-flowing probe vehicles. Probes with similar speeds are grouped together and a combinatorial algorithm estimates the time each group spent stalled, directly converting this to an estimate of the corresponding queue size. The study validates the method using historical traffic data and finds it accurately estimates queue sizes across various scenarios. Compared to traditional methods, it outperforms them in many cases, notably when traffic conditions change rapidly. The method works with any speed estimation system and requires only access to probe trajectories, making it a versatile and lightweight solution for real-world applications. The algorithm's efficiency allows it to be executed on limited-capacity edge devices, enabling real-time traffic state estimation on a large scale. The study further explores enhancing the method's precision by integrating the spatial distribution of probe vehicles and demonstrates the benefits of this approach. The combinatorial method's strengths make it suitable for concurrent queue size estimation and the detection of traffic incidents. The study demonstrates this potential by estimating the size of queues caused by incidents and finds the method compares favorably to existing approaches. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about these materials is limited due to the challenging analysis of their electronic characteristics. In a breakthrough, we successfully determined the electronic properties of Mn$_3$NiN layers by combining advanced experiments and simulations. Our findings revealed an exceptionally large anomalous Nernst coefficient in these layers, potentially enabling efficient thermal-to-electrical energy conversion without the need for magnetic fields. Next steps in research could involve optimizing the growth techniques to enhance device functionality and exploring similar effects in other antiperovskite materials. Moreover, our work highlights the potential of Mn$_3$NiN in various applications, including thermal sensors and Hall effect devices, and provides a foundation for investigating other antiferromagnetic materials in thin film forms.

The significant increase in computing requirements for artificial intelligence, despite its historical association with local processing, is evident in the present age of giant technology giants offering cloud-based AI services. This development has given rise to a new paradigm of 'AI in the middle', characterizing a broad range of applications that incorporate remote computing. In our work, we explore the potential of this middleware paradigm within the context of large-scale user centers, where massive groups of individuals contribute computing resources. We successfully implemented a system where users with varying levels of expertise can access remote computing resources, contribute to various volunteer computing projects, and leverage customizable workspace environments. Our findings reveal a 30-50% improvement in processing efficiency and high satisfaction rates among users, exceeding 90% in several categories. This research was conducted at the Harbin Institute of Technology, and the findings have implications for managing large-scale user centers, managing complex projects, and developing efficient workspace environments. We make our system's source code available to the public, inviting collaboration and potential applications in volunteer computing projects, cloud-based gaming, and remote educational platforms. This work has been presented at the IEEE International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Computing (ICAC 2022).

Based on the concept of topological insulation, random distributions of contact imperfections on a two-dimensional square lattice can create a path that allows electrons to circulate freely while skipping defective sites. In contextual linear gambits with $d$ dimensions, agents make decisions based on contextual information and learn a linear decision rule. The contextual parameters and rule coefficients are learned using stochastic gradient descent. We analyze a distributed learning model where multiple agents, each with their own contextual information, learn the contextual parameters and rule coefficients. However, they do not share the contextual information, and instead, the context is generated independently and identically across agents. We establish theoretical bounds on the learning rate of the contextual parameters and rule coefficients in a single-agent setting. For the distributed setting, we show that the optimal policy can be approximated by averaging the actions over agents, with guaranteed convergence rates. We also analyze a decentralized implementation of the learning model and provide guarantees on its convergence rates. Finally, we provide experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in various scenarios. The code for the experiments is available at https://github.com/ContextGambitLearning/CGRL. The paper contributes to the broader context of contextual linear gambits, which has applications in various areas such as contextual marketing, remote learning, and organizational teams. The main challenge in this setting is that the contextual information is generated independently and identically across agents, preventing them from sharing the context and learning the parameters and rule coefficients jointly. The paper proposes several appendices that provide additional details on the learning algorithm, the generation of contextual information, and the simulation experiments. The main theoretical and empirical results are presented in the main text. Our research involves examining the underlying assumptions of the event form encoding approach, which converts raw collision data into events for subsequent analysis, specifically for our study of the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC. By re-engineering event forms, we aim to explore the impact of initial conditions encoded in events on final particle distributions. Our analysis focuses on inclusive particle spectra and elliptic flow patterns in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy. Our re-encoded events, obtained using the TRENTO, MuQG, and SMOKER models, demonstrate a 10-30% variation in charged particle spectra and a 5-10% elliptic flow variation. Our study highlights the need for precise event form engineering to accurately capture the complex initial conditions of collisions. By re-encoding events using different models, we also gain valuable insights into the underlying physics of the ALICE experiment. This work investigates the extremal high-SNR behavior of a Gaussian interference network with $K$ users. Specifically, we examine the extremal values of the sum of user rates (sum-GDoF) in an interference network with variable power control, comparing those obtained using a binary power control scheme. Our main contribution is to establish upper and lower bounds on the sum-GDoF benefit of optimal power control over binary power control. These bounds hold for a wide range of SNR levels and provide the specific case where the average SNR per link is fixed at $\frac{1}{\Theta(\sqrt{K})}$. Furthermore, we show that the sum-GDoF benefit of optimal power control over binary power control initially increases, before entering a regime where it stabilizes and a second regime where it decreases, ultimately being bounded by $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for any $K \geq 4$. This article presents an innovative approach to achieving a better understanding of a specific Diophantine equation that has been extensively studied. Originally introduced by Alfred van der Poorten in 1980, the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ was a key component in his efforts to demonstrate the undeterminability of the constant $\gamma = 1+\sqrt{7}$. The structure and stability of dense stellar matter are scrutinized within dense stellar matter, which contains strange quarks, and this analysis is applied to dense stellar matter with two strains of quark: up, down, and strange. The necessary conditions for stability, which include negative pressure, zero bulk viscosity, and a positive speed of sound, are evaluated in various scenarios of quark density and composition. The outcome indicates that the speed of sound remains higher than 0.5 within all tested conditions, and even exceeds 0.6 in certain cases. Consequently, the constraint on the sound speed of approximately 0.5, frequently used in theoretical studies, appears too conservative. The dependence of the speed of sound on density and quark composition has been found to be relatively mild, with the sound speed being roughly constant across a broad range of densities. The outcome also supports compact star stability up to 2 solar masses, based on sound speed and density relationships, and suggests that the transition from conformal to non-conformal behavior occurs at a density range of approximately 3 to 6 times nuclear saturation density. The necessary conditions for stability are satisfied in various density regimes where the speed of sound drops to nearly 0.5, indicating that the sound speed of about 0.5 is likely a suitable cutoff in theoretical studies. The outcome can be applied to heavy neutron stars, as the sound speed remains high even at high densities, and therefore these stars should also be stable. The outcome has been derived from a quark model study involving up, down, and strange quarks, and the results are independent of specific models used. The outcome can be further validated by directly measuring the sound speed through astrophysical observations of compact stars. The desired measurement of the sound speed on compact stars, which should reflect the sound speed of dense stellar matter, can be carried out using existing data from the gravitational wave observatory. The outcome indicates that the sound speed of compact stars should fall within a range of approximately 0.48 to 0.52, which is compatible with the results of quark matter models involving up, down, and strange quarks. To effectively address the challenging open-domain commonsense question answering task, we introduce a novel approach, C2P, which focuses on gathering high-quality training data for our proposed model framework. This framework consists of two components: a basic neural network and a semantic-aware booster. We begin by establishing a rich semantic-aware pre-trained model as our base neural network. This base network is enhanced by the booster component, which draws upon hard negative examples and semantic-related information to create a more precise model. We achieve this by strategically selecting easier positive examples to form a coarse model and then use the booster component to incorporate the selected negative examples and semantic-related information into the model. We validate C2P on the Open-Domain Commonsense Question Answering dataset and observe significant improvements in accuracy when compared to conventional approaches. Moreover, our method demonstrates high levels of efficiency, efficacy, and robustness in critical aspects. We publicly release C2P at https://github.com/ghruan/C2P_CSA.

The findings indicate that only 13% of the observed spectra feature the characteristic patterns of known molecular cations, with many showing similarity to electron transition spectra of naphthalamine and its derivatives. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying framework that evaluates these methods remains unclear. Has difficulty in tackling this issue been overstated? Can the challenge of knowledge tracing be easily solved? We present a comprehensive textbook that addresses these misconceptions and delves into the complexities of this problem. It also introduces a Python-based framework, pyKT, that provides a clear breakdown of the framework's components and offers a practical application of the framework in the form of a neural network. Furthermore, we provide two novel deep learning-based approaches that directly address the cold-start issue and difficulty of modeling. One approach incorporates meta-pretraining and a novel module called a memory mixer, while the other uses a more complex neural network called a memory-based overparameterized network. Both of these methods demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in multiple simulation scenarios. All code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/pyKT.

The research also explores specific instances of the span property for various types of elliptic operators on specific manifolds. The paper includes an appendix containing a version of the slice theorem that can be utilized in this context. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing their updates can significantly reduce system efficiency. The asynchronous accumulation approach, which allows updates from devices to contribute to the model update at any time, has been shown to improve scalability while minimizing synchronization points. However, the challenge of gradient diversity that arises with unconstrained submissions can hinder the convergence of the model. We address this challenge by developing FedBA2, the first unconstrained, asynchronous learning algorithm to combine gradient buffering with asynchronous accumulation. FedBA2 generates a globally optimal model in a single phase, and we establish convergence bounds for two variants of the algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of FedBA2 in terms of convergence speed and system efficiency in comparative experiments. FedBA2 is particularly well-suited for large-scale, unconstrained, cross-device learning applications and supports an arbitrary number of devices. The code for FedBA2 is available at the website: https://github.com/lingwei-li/FedBA2.

We investigate self-gravitating relativistic objects composed of two fluids, one of which must remain nonisotropic to prevent it from becoming overdensed, while the other fluid can be isotropic. We determine the conditions under which a nonisotropic dual-fluid configuration could potentially exist by analyzing a range of parameters in this specific scenario. We also examine the effects of nonisotropy on the object's surface gravity and mass-radius relationships for various fluid compositions. Furthermore, we consider a simple model where the nonisotropic fluid's energy density varies with radius, which allows us to derive an approximate equation that enables us to map out the possible existence niches for these objects across a range of compactness values. We also explore the relationship between the objects' mass and their specific nonisotropic properties, discovering that only objects with a particular compactness range can exist and that even in the canonical Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff case, these objects have a similar compactness range. We additionally compare our results with existing research on the upper mass limit for self-gravitating objects in General Relativity, finding that the nonisotropic dual-fluid objects' mass limit fits within the range defined by these existing constraints. We also examine the objects' mass and surface gravity behavior in the regime where the objects' surface gravity exceeds their mass, finding that the nonisotropic dual-fluid objects' mass decreases at a slower rate than the square of their surface gravity in this scenario. We additionally analyze the objects' mass and surface gravity behavior in the regime where the objects' surface gravity is less than their mass, finding that the nonisotropic dual-fluid objects' mass decreases at a rate equal to the square of their surface gravity in this scenario. We derive these results through both numerical simulations and an analytical analysis of the objects' mass and surface gravity equations. We also examine the objects' mass and radius behavior in the regime where the objects' surface gravity is less than their mass, finding that the nonisotropic dual-fluid objects' radius decreases at a rate equal to half the rate of their mass in this scenario. We believe that the nonisotropic dual-fluid objects' mass and surface gravity behavior could be relevant to compact objects such as neutron stars and black holes, which are often modeled as isotropic objects but may have an inherent nonisotropic nature due to their complex internal composition. Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification models rely on vast amounts of labeled data for multiple domains. However, achieving domain agility with limited resources is crucial. This paper introduces a few-shot domain transfer approach, enabling models to seamlessly adapt to unfamiliar domains with minimal data. The proposed method leverages controlled relatedness between input and output sentences from the target domain, drawing upon constraints from parse trees. Specifically, it guides the encoder to focus on necessary linguistic changes between domains, thereby facilitating low-cost training and enabling efficient adaptation. Experimental results on NESV test sets demonstrate that this approach surpasses baseline performance in multiple domains, averaging a 1.4 CER score points improvement over the baseline. Furthermore, this model exhibits exceptional performance in synthetic experiments where it achieves a 2.3 CER score points increase over the baseline after adapting to a new domain. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghrua/gerd.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among agent trajectories. In particular, most current methods fail to adequately utilize positive trajectory data, thereby neglecting a wealth of valuable information. To address this limitation, this paper focuses on finding the most beneficial trajectory data among existing experiences and incorporates the most effective data into an apparatus for collective reinforcement learning through a system of interacting policy networks. By leveraging the strength of individual trajectories, our approach achieves higher levels of overall performance in comparison to conventional methods. Our solution is extensively evaluated in a range of offline environments, including multiple-agent navigation and multi-agent trading, and our approach is found to consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods across various scenarios. Our code has been made publicly accessible at https://github.com/ghru/PPMRL.

The alignment of megavoltage (MV) 2D/3D images is a complex task that can lead to suboptimal radiation treatment plans due to inaccuracies in patient positioning and image modulation measurements. A newly developed technique using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) successfully aligns MV images in 2D and 3D, achieving mean absolute errors of 4.85 mm and 6.07 mm respectively. When integrated into an optimization framework for radiation treatment planning, this technique leads to a 12% improvement in tumor control probability and a 15% reduction in liver normal tissue complication probability in 3D alignments, highlighting the significance of accurate image alignment in radiation treatment planning. A publicly available dataset is utilized to train and test the CNN, which demonstrates its potential for wide application in radiation treatment planning.

Using geometric information from the image of a black hole, we demonstrate that there is an essential limit to the rate at which mass can be lost, primarily due to the constraint that the accretion flow cannot exceed the speed of light. We show that, for a black hole, this limit results in a cap on the observable angle, which, in turn, imposes a maximum on the mass loss rate. Consequently, we derive a bond on the mass loss rate per unit energy, which can be observed as a upper boundary on the luminosity of a black hole. Based on the recently published SIMBOLOU imaging of the M87* black hole, we estimate this limit to be around 10^32 erg/s, which is comparable to its estimated spin-powered luminosity and highlights the significant impact of relativistic gravity on the observable properties of a black hole. This limit also implies that the fraction of mass lost per unit energy must be minimally 10^(-32) kg/erg, providing a novel insight into the behavior of matter at the event horizon. Finally, we discuss the implications of this result for accretion models, highlighting that any successful model must, as a minimum requirement, meet this mass loss limit in order to accurately capture the observed dynamics of a black hole. Lastly, we consider the possible applications of this finding to the imaging of the M87* black hole, suggesting that any future high-resolution observation that reveals the phasing of the bright side of the black hole must, inevitably, demonstrate a effect that is at the minimum equivalent to a 10% modulation of its luminosity. Ultimately, the significance of this result lies in its ability to constrain any theory that attempts to explain the behavior of a black hole, including its interactions with surrounding matter and energy.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 13 actions per second, largely because of strict safety checks required to prevent agents from exploiting exploited exploits.
In response to this challenge, we present TextWorldExpress, a high-speed text-based game that reaches an astonishing one million actions per second, surpassing the previous record by nearly 78 times.
TextWorldExpress maintains compatibility with popular text-based game frameworks like TextWorld and GlueText, ensuring seamless integration for existing agents, while also offering a range of challenging levels to test the limits of cutting-edge agents. 
Our results show that several renowned agents, including TextFooler, ReEnact, and TextBugHunter, exhibit a significant drop in performance in TextWorldExpress, with improvements in speed leading to increased gullibility and decreased effectiveness in detecting and exploiting vulnerabilities. 
Our findings suggest that evaluating agents on a limited set of low-speed text-based games may result in inaccurate assessments, and that a more precise evaluation requires faster frames of reference. 
Our code is available at github.com/sinewidget/textworldexpress.

Utilities are increasingly incorporating services from third-party providers for complementary activities such as wind power installation and electric vehicle charging.  These services create a loop where the utility purchases power and power in return is generated by the same installation, prompting a reevaluation of traditional procurement methods.  With an emphasis on sustainability and renewable energy, utilities are drawing towards procuring services rather than power alone.  Our paper explores the emerging pattern of services procurement by utilities and identifies key challenges, especially with regards to sustainability and renewable energy integration.  We then develop a robust procurement model for utility companies and two alternative hold-back strategies for a market structure featuring multiple generators.  Our numerical analysis validates the model's effectiveness across various scenarios and reveals interesting policy implications resulting from an increase in renewable generation, delayed installation of wind power, and altered risk preferences.  Our findings suggest that a sustainable procurement policy prioritizing renewable energy integration and reduced carbon footprint pays off in the long run.  We also discover an optimal threshold for a performance bond that maximizes utility execution and reduces risk.  Our research provides actionable insights for industry stakeholders, renewable energy policymakers, and regulators seeking to promote sustainable procurement and renewable energy integration.  We conclude by outlining potential avenues for future research on the complex and dynamic renewable energy sector. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence ranking for machine reading comprehension, our approach assesses sentence connections using discourse indicators' semantic meanings. This research introduces the DiscSense dataset, which contains the semantic properties of discourse indicators and our associated evaluation task. We've developed a learning-based system to accurately predict the sentence connections indicated by discourse markers. Our results show that combining discourse indicators' semantics with learning-based models enhances the performance of CommaSense, leading to a 2.3% improvement in F1-score. Furthermore, a case study illustrates how DiscSense facilitates the discovery of discourse indicators' semantic properties, revealing that many indicate causal relationships. We've made the DiscSense dataset and our code available at the specified URL.

Multilingual models are highly effective for natural language processing tasks when working with multiple languages, yet using a monolingual model requires significant resources to expand to a multilingual model. Current approaches to adapt a monolingual model to multilingual tasks involve multiple challenges: ensuring the model maintains linguistic independence, effectively leveraging resource-rich monolingual data, and successfully generalizing to target tasks across multiple languages. In response to these difficulties, this research introduces Cluster-consistent Multilingual Multitask Network (CMMNet), a novel framework constructing a multilingual shared semantic space from separate monolingual spaces while preserving linguistic independence. Furthermore, CMMNet incorporates a strategy to incorporate high-quality monolingual data while reducing cognitive load. Empirical evaluations validate the effectiveness of this framework, demonstrating significant improvements in multiple evaluation metrics. Interestingly, this research also uncovers intriguing findings indicating that monolingual models developed for low-resource languages can be readily expanded to high-resource languages with the cluster-consistent multilingual multitask network framework. All experiments were conducted using nine languages, including English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese, among others. All associated code has been publicly released on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zwang95/CMMNet. Moreover, a dedicated website is available at the following URL: http://zwang95.github.io/project/CMMNet.

This paper presents an examination of mid-rapidity particle production for Xe-Xe collisions at a nucleon-nucleon collision energy of 5.44 TeV, across a wide range of transverse momenta. Newly available data from the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC facility enable precise measurements of particle production rates in 13 micron barn collisions. Compared to Pb-Pb collisions at the same energy, particle production rates show similar patterns, with exceptions noted for $\phi$ mesons and proton and antiproton production, which exhibit different suppression levels. Additionally, particle production rates are found to be proportional to the number of collision participants rather than the total energy released in the collisions. Separate studies of strange and charm hadron production, as well as Philipps-sidends in the $\phi$ meson system, reveal consistent results with existing data. Two models, the Thermal-Statistical Model and the Cockloft Nuclear Reactions Model, are used to interpret the findings, with the latter highlighting unique characteristics of collision centralities. Separate analyses of the $\phi$ meson and its Philips-sidends also yield the first measurement of the $\phi$ meson's decay angle in proton-proton collisions, along with the first calculation of the $\phi$ meson's yield per collision in proton-proton collisions. The research was previously published in Physical Review Letters, with the exception of the $\phi$ meson decay angle analysis, which was published in Physics Letters B. The public availability date of the data is December 2021. The data and figures are now available for general use. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and VIO techniques provide a way to achieve this by learning from sensor data. Despite successful applications, VIO systems often struggle with temporal consistency and map representation. To overcome these challenges, we introduce EMA-VIO, a deep Visual-Inertial Navigation model that utilizes an external memory attention mechanism to dynamically balance between temporal and spatial awareness. This model ensures consistent tracking and map representation by incorporating adaptation weights derived from the current estimation and prediction tasks. Using the Inertial Measurement Unit, VIO can prevent map representation distortion and improve temporal consistency. We further propose a two-stage training method to enhance model generalization and adaptivity. Experimentation on the VIO-benchmark shows that EMA-VIO outperforms baseline VIO models in terms of localization accuracy and map representation consistency. Furthermore, we demonstrate the navigation system's ability to adapt to dynamic environments and provide accurate maps for future references. Comparative analysis with existing VIO models reveals that EMA-VIO achieves superior performance in terms of estimation errors and map representation quality. The proposed method's effectiveness is also validated through experiments on real-world navigation scenarios, showing that EMA-VIO can be applied in various mobile navigation situations. The code for EMA-VIO is available at https://github.com/JinPengPeng/EMA-VIO.

These experiments demonstrate how our method can effectively recover complete data from incomplete information. We have also compared our method's performance with the classical least squares approach and found that the quasi-reversibility technique provides a more accurate recovery of missing data. Furthermore, we have analyzed the stability and convergence of our method, and have also derived error estimates for the recovery of the missing data. We have conducted experiments to illustrate the feasibility of FedSI and identify suitable methods to enhance its efficiency. We then develop three algorithms tailored to FedSI: Weighted Average, Transfer Learning, and Deep Learning-based variants. Our proposed solutions are evaluated in three distinct scenarios, yielding promising results that match or exceed conventional machine learning standards. To facilitate comparison and validation, our code has been made publicly available. We have also established a baseline for future FedSI research by incorporating the results into the Federated Learning Benchmark. This work can be extended in several ways, including FedSI-based classification and more sophisticated learning models. Furthermore, we have appended a section on potential future directions for FedSI. Lastly, we have included a code example for FedSI using TensorFlow Federated. We investigate the accuracy of quantum parametrization methods by analyzing the identifiability of a quantum state's parameter within a specific time frame, known as the identifiability time. This research considers the simplification of the quantum speed limit (QSL) inequality, Asymmetry Monotone (AM), to explore the identifiability time frame for a single qubit.
